title: Identification of N-glycosylation sites on HHV glycoprotein B trimers (HSV-1, EBV, HCMV)
projectDescription: Mass spectrometry data for the identification and characterization of N-glycosylation sites on herpesvirus glycoprotein B (gB) trimers. gB proteins were analyzed by LC-MS/MS following proteolytic digestion, with PNGase F-treated and untreated samples analyzed to identify N-glycosylated peptides and assess site occupancy. The dataset includes HCD fragmentation spectra used to support the identification of N-glycosylation sites across gB. Examined protein include HSV-1 gB, EBV gB, and HCMV gB.
dataProcessingProtocol: Generated RAW files were searched using the MaxQuant (2.0.3.0) search software. The data was searched against the HHV gB sequences and a background canonical human protein sequence FASTA file from UNIPROT (UP000005640_9606, February 2021 release). Two missed cleavages, methionine oxidation and asparagine deamidation were allowed as variable modifications with carbamidomethylation of cysteines set as a fixed modification. The output was filtered based on a 0.01 precursor false discovery rate. Asparagine deamination sites specific to each HHV gB sequence were then used in combination with peptide mass differences between the N-glycan cleaved and non-cleaved samples to identify N-glycosylation sites.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Mass spectrometry Six 20 µg samples including HHV-6A gB, HHV-7 gB, and KSHV gB, with or without N-glycans, were further purified using a ProteoExtract Protein Precipitation kit (MilliporeSigma). Samples were then diluted by an addition of 95 µl of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, reduced with DTT, carbidomethylated with 20mM iodoacetamide, and digested with 1 µg trypsin overnight. 4 µl of acetic acid was added to stop the reaction. Following trypsin digestion and inactivation, samples were C18 desalted, vacuum concentrated and dried by SpeedVac, and resuspended in 15 µl 1% formic acid. To analyze purified protein-derived tryptic peptides, 1 or 2 micrograms of measured total protein equivalent was subjected to in-line chromatography using an EASY-nLC 1200 System.For DDA MS data acquisition, the Q exactive HF instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used, with each cycle involving one full MS scan (at 60,000 resolution) followed by MS/MS scans (at 15,000 resolution) of the top 15 most abundant peaks (10 s dynamic exclusion time). The AGC target was set to 3e6 for full MS scans and 1e5 for MS/MS scans, with a maximum injection time of 75ms for full MS scans, 25ms for MS2 scans, and a normalized collision energy of 27 for MS/MS scans with a 200 to 2000 m/z range. The MS2 isolation window was set to 1.4 m/z.

title: Characterisation of prostate cancer sialome re-engineering via CMAH transfection
projectDescription: This study investigated sialome re-engineering in prostate cancer cells following transfection with the rat Cmah gene, which encodes cytidine monophosphate-N-acetylneuraminic acid hydroxylase (CMAH). Expression of rat CMAH enables the conversion of CMP-Neu5Ac to CMP-Neu5Gc. Glycoproteomic analysis was performed to characterise changes in sialylated glycopeptides in wild-type and rat Cmah-transfected LNCaP prostate cancer cells. The resulting glycopeptides were analysed by LC–MS/MS using an Orbitrap Fusion mass spectrometer, and glycopeptide assignments were obtained using Byonic. The dataset supports the characterisation of Neu5Gc-containing glycopeptides generated following CMAH-mediated sialome re-engineering. Sample E017 represents wild-type LNCaP cells, whereas sample E143 represents LNCaP cells transfected with the rat Cmah gene. For each sample, the RAW and Byonic result files sharing the same sample identifier correspond to the same LC–MS/MS analysis.
dataProcessingProtocol:
Peptides were analysed by LC–MS/MS over a 2 h acquisition period. Peptide separation was performed using a 50 cm EasyNano PepMap column, with flow delivered by a Waters mClass UPLC system. Data were acquired using an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid mass spectrometer operated in data-dependent acquisition (DDA) mode. High-resolution MS1 spectra were acquired in the Orbitrap mass analyser, while rapid MS2 spectra were acquired following higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) in the ion trap mass analyser using a 1 s top-speed cycle.

Spectra were searched against the human subset of the UniProt Swiss-Prot database (UniProt_human_SP_20180123_validated.fasta) using Byonic. The E017 and E143 datasets were searched using Byonic v4.4.2 and v5.0.20-g02838203, respectively. β-Methylthiolation of cysteine was set as a fixed modification to account for alkylation. Oxidation of methionine and N-terminal acetylation were set as common variable modifications. A total of 78 O-glycan and 309 N-glycan structures representing known mammalian glycan configurations were included as rare variable modifications.

Protein-level results were filtered to require a minimum of two unique peptides and a global false discovery rate (FDR) of 1%, assessed empirically using a decoy database. Peptide-level results were similarly filtered at a 1% FDR and were additionally restricted to individual peptide-spectrum matches with a log probability greater than 1.3 (P < 0.05).
sampleProcessingProtocol: Approximately 1.0 × 10⁶ cells (50–100 µg glycoprotein) were harvested using PBS and gentle pipetting. Cell pellets were lysed at room temperature in five volumes of freshly prepared SDS-containing lysis buffer. The lysates were mixed by repeated pipetting and were not cooled on ice to avoid precipitation. Proteins were reduced with TCEP and alkylated with methyl methanethiosulfonate (MMTS). Protein samples were subsequently processed using an S-Trap procedure and digested with a mixture of trypsin and Lys-C. The resulting peptide mixtures were collected for LC–MS/MS analysis.

title: surface proteome of WT vs. MGAT1 KO HeLa cells
projectDescription: Using cell-surface biotinylation followed by mass spectrometry (MS), we revealed substantial differences between the surface proteomes of WT and MGAT1 KO HeLa cells. Among the most strongly depleted proteins in MGAT1 KO cells were those involved in cell adhesion and extracellular interactions, membrane domain organization, and cytoskeletal organization. These include LGALS3 (galectin-3) that cross-links complex N-glycans thus stabilizes these glycoproteins at the surface27; ITGA4, ITGA7 (integrin- α4 and α7), matrix adhesion receptors that also contribute to raft stabilization through their clustering and scaffolding; ICAM1, MCAM, and BCAM that mediate cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions; and CAVIN1, the caveolae-associated scaffolding protein that is essential, together with LGALS3, for caveolae biogenesis. These observations suggest that MGAT1 loss broadly compromises the integrity of host cell membrane microdomain.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw data were processed in MaxQuant (v2.1.3.0) with the Andromeda search engine against the human UniProt database, using standard parameters (Cys carbamidomethylation; Met oxidation and N-terminal acetylation as variable modifications; 1% FDR at peptide/protein level; minimum 7 aa; up to two missed cleavages). Label-free quantification was performed using MaxLFQ49, and statistical analyses were carried out in Perseus
sampleProcessingProtocol: WT and MGAT1 KO HeLa cells were selectively labeled using a membrane-impermeable sulfo-NHS-biotin (EZ-Link™ Sulfo-NHS-Biotin, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were cultured in 6-well plates to ~90% confluence. Following two washes with ice-cold PBS, cells were incubated on ice for 1 h with Sulfo-NHS-SS-Biotin or PBS for negative control. Excess NHS-biotin was quenched by two sequential washes with TBS, followed by one additional wash with cold PBS. Cells were then scraped from the plate and lysed in 1% Triton X-100 and biotinylated proteins were enriched by incubating the lysate with streptavidin-agarose beads for 1 h at RT with gentle rotation. Beads were washed extensively with PBS and subjected to proteolysis and mass spectrometry (MS) analysis. Proteolysis and LC-MS/MS were done by the Smoler Proteomics Center at the Israel Institute of Technology. Briefly, beads were washed and subjected to on-bead digestion in 2 M urea, 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate with reduction (10 mM DTT, 60 °C, 30 min) and alkylation (10 mM iodoacetamide, 30 min, dark). Proteins were digested overnight at 37 °C with modified trypsin (Promega), followed by a second 4 h digestion. Peptides were desalted using Oasis HLB µElution plates, dried, and re-suspended in 0.1% formic acid/2% acetonitrile. Peptides were analyzed by LC-MS/MS on a Q Exactive HF-X coupled to an Ultimate 3000 UHPLC. Samples were loaded onto a 30-cm C18 column and eluted using a 5–28% acetonitrile gradient over 60 min, followed by column washing. MS1 scans were acquired at 60,000 resolution (m/z 300–1500) and MS2 scans at 15,000 resolution using HCD (NCE 27). Dynamic exclusion was set to 20 s.

title: Crosslinking mass spectrometry of the α/β subunit interface in urinary and recombinant human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
projectDescription: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a heterodimeric glycoprotein hormone whose urinary (u-hCG) and recombinant (r-hCG) forms differ in glycosylation and stability. To test whether this reflects a structural reorganization of the α/β subunit interface, the two forms were compared by chemical crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS). Crosslinking was performed on the intact, natively glycosylated heterodimers using two complementary chemistries: the lysine-reactive reagent DSS and the zero-length coupling reagent DMTMM (targeting Lys-Asp/Glu pairs, each in biological triplicate for both forms. Identified inter-subunit crosslinks were mapped onto the hCG structure to evaluate whether the assembled core interface is conserved between u-hCG and r-hCG. The dataset comprises the raw LC-MS/MS files and the corresponding crosslink identifications for all conditions and replicates, and accompanies a broader native-MS, ion-mobility and collision-induced-unfolding study of the two hCG forms.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw files were converted to mzXML and searched with xQuest (v2.1.5) against a database of 26 sequences comprising the hCG α and β subunits, sample-preparation enzymes (Lys-C, trypsin, PNGase F) and common contaminants, together with reversed-sequence decoys. Searches used trypsin specificity (up to 2 missed cleavages), peptide length 4-40, fixed cysteine carbamidomethylation, and variable methionine oxidation and asparagine deamidation (conversion of Asn to Asp at formerly N-glycosylated sites), and precursor and fragment tolerances were ±15 ppm. DSS was searched as a Lys/N-terminus crosslink (+138.0681 Da); DMTMM as a zero-length Lys-to-Asp/Glu amide bond (-18.0106 Da). Crosslink-spectrum matches were filtered to mass error ≤5 ppm, TIC score >=0.1, Δscore <0.9, ≥5 matched fragment ions per peptide, and identification in ≥2 of 3 biological replicates. Cα-Cα distances for inter-subunit crosslinks were evaluated against the hCG crystal structure (PDB 1HRP) and an AlphaFold model.  Further information can be found in the accompanying publication.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Crosslinking was performed on intact, natively glycosylated u-hCG and recombinant hCG (10 µg) in 25 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 1 h at 25 °C, in three independent biological replicates per condition. For amine-reactive crosslinking, an equimolar mixture of isotopically light and heavy DSS (DSS-d0/d12) in dimethylformamide was added to 1 mM and quenched with ammonium bicarbonate (50 mM). For zero-length crosslinking, DMTMM was added to 10 mM and excess reagent removed on Zeba Spin columns. Samples were resuspended in ammonium bicarbonate with 0.02% ProteaseMAX; N-glycans were removed with PNGase F. Proteins were reduced with TCEP, alkylated with iodoacetamide, and digested sequentially with Lys-C (1:100, 3 h) and trypsin (1:50, overnight) at 37 °C. Peptides were desalted on Sep-Pak C18. LC-MS/MS was performed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos coupled to an EASY-nLC 1200 (75 µm × 25 cm C18 column, 72 min gradient). MS1 was acquired at 120,000 resolution; precursors of charge 3-7 were isolated and fragmented by CID (35% NCE), with MS2 acquired in the Orbitrap at 30,000 resolution. Further information can be found in the accompanying publication.

title: Screening of the transcriptome, mucinome, and O‐/N‐glycans of the intestinal goblet cell model HT29‐MTX during zinc deficiency
projectDescription: Zinc deficiency is a global health problem affecting approximately one billion people and is associated with serious health consequences, including impaired immune function and an increased susceptibility to infections and inflammation. It is also linked to disrupted intestinal homeostasis and a higher incidence of diarrheal diseases. In addition to the severe degeneration of the intestinal epithelium observed during zinc deficiency, the mucus barrier in the intestinal tract is also disrupted. Intestinal mucus does not only protect the underlying epithelium and provides a habitat for the commensal microbiota, it also plays a critical role in the absorption of trace elements such as zinc. Our previous studies conducted using the human goblet cell model HT29-MTX already indicated that zinc deficiency alters the intestinal O-glycome, as the gene expression of several mucins and glycosyltransferases (GTFs) was dysregulated and the O-glycosylation pattern of mucins secreted by the cells were changed, with a significant increase of shorter glycans. However, the consequences of these observations for the entire mucin O-glycome remain to be fully investigated.
dataProcessingProtocol: Samples were analyzed by online nanoflow liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry using an Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) coupled to a Dionex UltiMate 3000 HPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). For each analysis, 2 µL was injected onto an Acclaim PepMap 100 column packed with 2 cm of 5 µm C18 material (164564, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) using 0.1% formic acid in water (solvent A). Peptides were then separated on a 15 cm PepMap RSLC EASY-Spray C18 column packed with 2 µm C18 material (ES904, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) using a gradient from 0-35% solvent B (0.1% formic acid with 80% ACN) in 60 min. Full scan MS1 spectra were collected at a resolution of 60,000, an automatic gain control target of 3e5, and a mass range from m/z 300 to 1500. Dynamic exclusion was enabled with a repeat count of 2, repeat duration of 7 s, and exclusion duration of 7 s. Only charge states 2 to 6 were selected for fragmentation. MS2s were generated at top speed for 3 seconds. Higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) was performed on all selected precursor masses with the following parameters: isolation window of 2 m/z, 29% normalized collision energy, Orbitrap detection (resolution of 7,500), maximum inject time of 50 ms, and a standard automatic gain control target. An additional electron transfer dissociation (ETD) fragmentation of the same precursor was triggered if 1) the precursor mass was between m/z 300 to 1500 and 2) 3 of 8 N-acetylhexosamine (HexNAc) or N-acetylneuraminic acid (NeuAc) fingerprint ions (126.055, 138.055, 144.07, 168.065, 186.076, 204.086, 274.092, and 292.103) were present at m/z ± 0.1 and greater than 5% relative intensity. Two files were collected for each sample: the first collected an ETD scan with supplemental energy (EThcD) while the second method collected a scan without supplemental energy. Both used charge-calibrated ETD reaction times, 100 ms maximum injection time, and standard injection targets. EThcD parameters were as follows: Orbitrap detection (resolution 7,500), calibrated charge-dependent ETD times, 15% nCE for HCD, maximum inject time of 150 ms, and a standard 342 precursor injection target. For the second file, dependent scans were only triggered for 343 precursors below m/z 1000, and data were collected in the ion trap using a normal scan rate. Raw files were searched using Byonic (version 4.5.2, Protein Metrics, Inc.) against the UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot Homo sapiens proteome (Query: proteome:up000005640 AND reviewed:true) and a curated mucin database. Briefly, the mucin database consists of nearly 349 350 proteins from Uniprot’s annotated human proteome predicted to bear the dense O-glycosylation characteristic of mucin domains. For all samples, we used the default O-glycan database containing 9 common structures. Raw files were first searched against the human proteome and then the curated mucin database. In both cases, files were searched with semi-specific cleavage N-terminal to Ser and Thr and six allowed missed cleavages. Samples treated with trypsin were searched with the same parameters but also allowed cleavage C-terminal to Arg or Lys. Mass tolerance was set to 10 ppm for MS1’s and 20 ppm for MS2’s. Met oxidation was set as a variable modification and carbamidomethyl Cys was set as a fixed modification. From the Byonic search results, glycopeptides were filtered to a score of >150 and a logprob of >1. Mucins ranked higher than the second Byonic protein-level reverse hit were considered true identifications. Protein intensities were extracted from the Byonic output and normalized by the normalization factor based on the total summed intensity of the top 500 ranked proteins identified within the same proteomic dataset to correct for sample loading and measurement variation. The normalized intensities were averaged within each triplicate and used to highlight the five mucins with the highest mean signal intensities; the remaining mucins were grouped as “others.” The area under the extracted ion chromatogram (XIC) peak for a representative tryptic peptide from each mucin (MUC2: ¹¹⁷⁰DRPIYEEDLKK¹¹⁸⁰; MUC5B: ²³⁴⁶AAGGAVCEQPLGLECR²³⁶¹; MUC17: ³⁴AVWDGGGCISQGDVLNR⁵⁰; MUC5AC: 56GATVFPSLR64) was normalized to the intensity of a reference peptide from SmE (¹¹⁹RGENEAAFFAR¹²⁹) within the same sample.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The pET28 plasmids for His-tagged SmEnhancin and StcE were kindly provided by the Bertozzi laboratory. Following the protocol published in Mahoney et al. 26. StcEE447D was conjugated to NHS-activated beads and washed 3× with 1 mL of PBS followed by the addition of the proteins, which were allowed to bind overnight at 4 °C. Free NHS-esters were capped by adding 100 mM Tris, pH 7.4, to the bead slurry and incubated for 3 hours at 4 °C. After capping, beads were washed 3x with a high-salt buffer (20 mM Tris and 500 mM NaCl) followed by a buffer without salt (20 mM Tris). HT-29-MTX cell lysates and media (supernatant) were filtered through a 0.22 μm vacuum filter (Merck Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA), concentrated using Amicon Ultra centrifugal filters (30 kDa MWCO, Merck Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA), and analyzed by BCA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) to determine protein concentration. 2 mg of samples were brought to a final volume of 500 μL in no-salt buffer, and Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) was added to a final concentration of 1 mM. The protein-conjugated solid supports (100 μL) were added to the samples and allowed to rotate at 4 °C overnight. After binding, the beads were washed 3× with the high-salt buffer and 2× with the no-salt buffer. Bound proteins were eluted by adding 100 μL of 0.5% sodium deoxycholate (SDC) in 20 mM Tris and boiling the beads at 95 °C with agitation. The elution step was repeated once, and the two eluates were pooled. Following elution, the enriched samples were subjected to reduction, alkylation, and proteolytic digestion. To begin, dithiothreitol (DTT) was added to a concentration of 1 mM and allowed to react at 65 °C for 20 min followed by alkylation in 1.5 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) for 15 min in the dark at RT. Subsequently, 800 ng of mucinase SmE was added and allowed to react overnight at 37 °C, then subjected to an additional digestion with 100 ng of trypsin (Promega, Fitchburg, WI, USA) for 6 h at 37 °C. All reactions were quenched by adding 1 μL of formic acid (85178, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and diluted to a volume of 200 μL prior to desalting. The addition of formic acid also caused SDC to precipitate out of the solution, and the resulting supernatant was transferred to a new tube before desalting. Desalting was performed using 10 mg Strata-X 33 μm polymeric reversed-phase solid-phase extraction (SPE) columns (8B-S100-AAK, Phenomenex, Torrance, CA, USA). Each column was activated using 500 μL of acetonitrile (ACN) (LC015, Honeywell, Charlotte, NC, USA) followed by 500 μL of 0.1% formic acid, 500 μL of 0.1% formic acid in 40% ACN, and equilibration with two additions of 500 μL of 0.1% formic acid. After equilibration, the samples were added to the column and rinsed twice with 200 μL of 0.1% formic acid. The columns were transferred to a 1.5 mL tube for elution by two additions of 150 μL of 0.1% formic acid in 40% ACN. The eluent was then dried by using a vacuum concentrator (LabConco, Kansas City, MO, USA) prior to reconstitution in 8 μL of 0.1% formic acid.

Glycoproteomics identify disease-associated N-glycans and reduced occupancy of glycosylation sites in PMM2-CDG
projectDescription: The routine diagnostic pathway for congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) relies on carbohydrate deficient transferrin, a test that incompletely captures defects in N linked glycosylation and may yield false negative results even in classical N glycosylation disorders such as PMM2 CDG. To explore molecular features of CDG pathogenesis and thereby novel biomarker candidates, we applied an integrated quantitative LC–MS/MS glycoproteomic workflow to a well characterised cohort of individuals with PMM2 CDG (n = 7) and MPI CDG (n = 2), alongside controls. The workflow combines the analysis of N-glycopeptides and corresponding non-glycosylated peptides in serum and plasma. Distinct disease associated glycosylation patterns were observed in PMM2 CDG. Elevated levels of immature mannose-type (paucimannose-like) N-glycans were detected at specific sites, including GlcNAc(2)Man(4) at Asn 85 of complement component 3, GlcNAc(2)Man(3) at Asn 869 of α 2 macroglobulin, and GlcNAc(2)Man(5) at Asn 226 of complement component 4. In parallel, approximately 50 peptides with unoccupied N glycosylation sequons, including peptides from transferrin, were recurrently identified in CDG patient samples, indicating widespread reductions in N glycosylation site occupancy. Together, this cohort based glycoproteomic analysis reveals coherent, site specific disruptions in protein glycosylation that reflect underlying defects in mannose metabolism in PMM2 CDG. These molecular features define candidate glycophenotypes with potential utility as biomarkers for CDG subtype discrimination, disease stratification, and assessment of disease severity in future studies.
dataProcessingProtocol: Data analysis was performed with Proteome Discoverer version 3.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the Byonic search engine (v. 4.3.4, Protein Metrics) towards the human Uniprot database (20 042 entries). The N-glycan modifications were set to 204 compositions ranging from HexNAc(1) to HexNAc(7)Hex(8)Fuc(1)NeuAc(4). One glycan was allowed per peptide (common1 setting), but additional analyses were performed using two allowed glycans and the common2 setting. Additional dynamic modifications were Met oxidation and loss of NH2 from N-terminal Gln and Cys, where one of these were allowed per peptide (rare1 setting); and finally fixed carbamidomethyl group of Cys. Allowed peptide cleavage sites were after Lysine (K) and Arginine (R), including two missed cleavages, and the mass accuracy limit was 5 ppm for precursor ions and 20 ppm for MS2 ions. The false discovery rate was set to 1% and an additional protein-aware posterior error probability (PEP2D) score of <0.001 was used in the initial filtering of GPSMs and PSMs. Selected glycopeptide MS2 spectra were manually verified to contain peaks confirming the matched peptide (Y0), peptide+HexNAc (Y1) and peptide+HexNAcFuc (core-fucosylated N-glycans) ions. Also, the proper set of diagnostic saccharide oxonium ions had to be present, for instance, presence of m/z 274.09 for compositions including Neu5Ac and m/z 163.06 at >20% relative abundance (at 20-30% NCEs) for compositions including oligomannose N-glycosylation. For the GPSM-based relative quantification analyses, PCA-plots and volcano plots, the two replicate measurements of the HILIC samples made at 38% NCE were summed and used. The identification of non-glycosylated peptides of N-glycopeptides also detected in the same sample was assessed by adding the GPSMs from the two HILIC runs (NCE 38%), to the PSMs and GPSMs of the two non-HILIC runs (NCE 30%) and then filtering for the simultaneous presence of GPSMs and non-glycosylated PSMs sharing the same peptide sequence. After filtering for glycopeptide (glycan composition contains Hex), the Peptide groups, Minora consensus features and PSM tables were imported into R-studio for processing. Data was summarised by aggregating spectrum counts at the glycosylation site level (>1 GPSM identity threshold), protein level (>2 GPSM identity threshold), and at the glycan composition level. The resulting summary tables were exported to excel spreadsheets for further analysis and visualisation. Relative glycoform abundances were assayed by summing GPSMs for each glycan/glycopeptide and normalizing to the total GPSM signal or to selected glycoproteins/N-glycosylation sites within each sample, enabling comparisons and statistical analyses across samples.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Plasma and serum samples were obtained from 9 patients with PMM2- and MPI-CDG diagnoses, established from serum TF and genetic analyses. Samples were collected at the Clinical Chemistry Laboratory, Sahlgrenska University, Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden. Li-heparin plasma control samples (n=9) were obtained from the same laboratory after analysis of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH). The control individuals were aged 3 months to 58 years, collected to match the ages of the CDG cases. This study was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (EPN 2023-06761-0) and specific informed consent was waived. Plasma/serum sample aliquots (6 µL) were added to digestion buffer (50 µL end volume) containing a final concentration of 0.1% SDOC, 50 mM TEAB and 10 mM DTT. The reduction was performed at 56 °C for 20 min, and then cysteine alkylation proceeded with 20 mM IAA at room temperature for 30 min in the dark; and finally, a new portion of 10 mM DTT was added, and the quenching of IAA was done for 15 min. An additional portion of 35 µL TEAB (100 mM) was added, and the protein digestion was performed at 37 °C for 14 h with trypsin/LysC mixture (Promega), at 50:1 substrate:enzyme ratio (approximating 0.4 mg protein in each sample) in an end volume of 100 µL. A second incubation was then done with trypsin (sequencing grade, Thermo Scientific) at 50:1 for 3.5 h at 37 °C . After proteolysis the samples were subjected to HiPPR detergent removal resin bulk material (0.4 mL per sample, Thermo Scientific) according to instructions. The samples were then acidified with trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) to pH <2 to precipitate remaining SDOC, centrifuged at 1000xg for 3 min and the supernatants subjected to C18 spin columns (Thermo Scientific) according to instructions. The elution of peptides was done with 2x100 µL 40% acetonitrile in ultrapure water. Each sample was divided into a ¼ fraction and a ¾ fraction and dried in a vacuum centrifuge at room temperature. The ¾ fractions were re-dissolved in 200 µL 80% acetonitrile / 1% TFA and subjected to zvitterionic hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (Zic-HILIC) for the enrichment of glycopeptides. The in-house packed spin columns contained 80 mg Zic-HILIC particles (10 μm porous silica, 200 Å; Sequant/Merck) and the samples were applied and re-applied four times with centrifugations at 1000g. Each column was then washed once with 250 µL of 80 % acetonitrile, 1 % TFA. Enriched glycopeptides were eluted with 3x60 µL of 0.1 % TFA followed by 60 μL of 25 mM TEAB and finally by 60 μL of 70 % acetonitrile; and then dried by vacuum centrifugation at room temperature.  For the LC-MS/MS analysis, the HILIC enriched glycopeptide and the non-HILIC peptide samples were dissolved in 60 µL and 90 µL 3% acetonitrile, 0.1% TFA, respectively. The samples were analysed on an Orbitrap Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) interfaced with the Easy-nLC1200 chromatography system (Thermo Scientific). The ion-transfer tube temperature was 275 °C and the positive ion spray voltage was 2 kV. Analytes (2 μL injection volume for HILIC samples and 1 µL for non-HILIC samples) were trapped on an Acclaim Pepmap 100 C18 trap column (100 μm x 2 cm, particle size 5 μm, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and separated on an in-house packed analytical column (75 μm x 45 cm, particle size 3 μm, Reprosil-Pur C18, Dr. Maisch), maintained in a temperature-control sleeve at 50 °C. The mobile phases were solvent A (0.2 % formic acid in water) and solvent B (80 % acetonitrile, 0.2 % formic acid in water); and the flow rate was 300 nL/min. The elution gradient started with 5 % B, going to 8 % B over 5 min, followed by an increase to 35 % B over 68 min, to 45% B over 5 min, to 100% B over 2 min and then remained at 100 % B for 15 min. The MS1 scans were acquired at 120 000 resolution with a m/z 600-2200 range (HILIC samples) or m/z 400-2000 (non-HILIC samples), and the most abundant 2-7 charged precursor ions were selected for fragmentation using higher-energy collision induced dissociation (HCD) with a duty cycle of 3 s and an isolation window of 3 m/z units (3 Th). The HILIC samples from patients were analysed with triplicate injections where the first injection was analysed with 20% and 30% normalized collision energy (NCE) in the m/z 109-2400 range (to include the diagnostic His immonium ion at m/z 110.07). The second and third injections were analysed with 38 % NCE in m/z 200-2000 range. For the non-HILIC samples, 30% NCE was used in the m/z 109-2000 range. The exclusion time was 12 s, precursor intensity threshold for MS2 was 5x104, MS2 resolution was 30 000, and maximum injection time was 90 ms. Two blank injections with isopropanol:acetonitrile:water (1:1:1) and solvent A were performed in between samples from different individuals to minimise and monitor any carry-over of analytes.

Glycan bead precipitation of proteins from Toxoplasma gondii lysate
projectDescription: Apicomplexan parasites use two sets of specialized organelles to invade mammalian host cells, the micronemes and the rhoptries. Microneme proteins mediate adhesion and interaction with host cell surfaces and upon appropriate contact mediate discharge of rhoptry organelles. Injection of rhoptry contents into host cells prepares the host cell for invasion and intracellular replication. We discovered that host galactose-containing N-glycans are required for rhoptry discharge from the apicomplexan Toxoplasma gondii, though the corresponding interacting microneme protein was unknown. Here, we identify the parasite proteins able interact with galactose and lactose.  We used agarose beads coated with lactose and galactose to precipitating the specific interactors from whole-parasite lysate. Mannose coated beads were used as a negative control due to host mannose being inconsequential in the rhoptry discharge process. The microneme proteins MIC1, MIC4, and MIC6 were identified as the primary strong interactors of both galactose and lactose. Follow up analysis confirmed their importance to rhoptry discharge and parasite invasion via their interactions with galactose-containing N-glycans. This is the first such host-parasite interaction discovered in Toxoplasma to regulate rhoptry discharge.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw files for each condition and replicate were analyzed using Proteome Discoverer 2.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The sequence database search was performed using Sequest HT with the optional search modifications including Oxidation (M), Deamidation (N,Q), Phosphorylation (S,T,Y), and Hexose (S,T,W). Precursor ions-based quantification was used with low abundance resampling for missing value imputation.
sampleProcessingProtocol: T. gondii RH/Δku80/Δhxgprt/dTomato parasites were grown in 15 cm2 plates of confluent HFF cells for 2 days. Parasites were harvested, filtered with 5 μm pore filters to remove host cells and debris, washed 2X with PBS via pelleting (5 min, 2000 g) and resuspension. After the final PBS wash was removed, the pellet was flash frozen in liquid N2. Pellets were lysed on ice by thawing directly into cold SugarAP buffer (PBS with 1 mM CaCl2, MgCl2, 0.5% Igepal CA-630, 1 mM benzonase [Millipore; E1014-25KU], and 1X protease inhibitor cocktail [Thermo; 87786]). While parasites were lysing, 200 μL bead slurry (100 μL final bed) of D-mannose agarose (Sigma; M6400), D-galactose agarose (Pierce; PI20372), and α-lactose agarose were added to empty spin columns (Pierce; 89879) and prepared by washing with 10 gel-bed volumes (4x250 μL) of SugarAP buffer; 40 g spins were used throughout for all steps. The parasite lysate was clarified by a centrifugation to remove insoluble debris (4°C, 11000 g, 10 min), and the soluble lysate flowed over each resin. Resins were washed for a total of 20 gel-bed volumes (8x 250 μL) using SugarAP buffer. Bound proteins were then specifically eluted by 100 mM of the free cognate sugar in SugarAP buffer (i.e. mannose, galactose, lactose), using 7.5 gel-bed volumes (3x 250 μL). Eluted proteins were prepared for mass spectrometry by SP3 bead digestion and clean-up as previously described (Hughes et al, 2019). Briefly, proteins were reduced with TCEP (Pierce, PI20490) and alkylated with chloroacetamide (Thermo, 148415000), precipitated onto hydrophilic and hydrophobic SP3 beads using ethanol, washed in 80% ethanol, and digested overnight with Trypsin/LysC mix (Thermo, A40007). Eluted peptides were lyophilized and directly injected without further cleanup in for DDA mass spectrometry on a Thermo Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer equipped with a FAIMS Pro Interface.  Two biological replicates were prepared and injected for each sugar sample condition.

title: A unified HILIC-FLD-MS workflow for simultaneous peptide and released N-glycan mapping of protein biopharmaceuticals
projectDescription: The study explored peptide mapping and released/RFMS-labeled N-glycan profiling in a single HILIC-FLD-MS chromatographic run as an alternative to separate peptide RPLC-MS mapping and HILIC-FLD assay of labeled glycans. Individual LC data files are annotated in the DataDescription.xlsx file.
dataProcessingProtocol: MS spectra were searched in Byonic v3.5.0 against the individual FASTA sequences of biopharmaceuticals or a 5-protein combined library, all appended with common contaminants. The mass tolerance was 10 ppm for precursors and 18 ppm for fragments. A fully or semispecific cleavage with two missed cleavages was used. Oxidized Met, deamidated Asn, ammonia loss from Asn, pyroGlu formation from N-terminal Glu and Gln, and dehydrated Asp were set as dynamic modifications. The search space included a built-in Byonic library of 164 mammalian N-glycan compositions uploaded to the repository as .XLSX files. Carbamidomethylation of Cys was set as a static modification. Peptide-spectrum matches identified with a 2D FDR ≤ 1%  were considered.  The spectra assigned to fully tryptic peptides were processed in Skyline, considering three monoisotopic peaks and precursor charge states ranging from 1+ to 6+.  Annotation of labeled glycans was performed in Skyline using targeted MS1 filtering based on the Byonic library described above, with precursor m/z values adjusted for RFMS labeling. Spectra were filtered with a 5 ppm mass tolerance, charge states 1+ to 3+, and extraction of three monoisotopic peaks. Glycans with similar precursor masses were distinguished using Neu5Ac+ oxonium fragments to identify sialylated species, and Y1/Y2 ions corresponding to RFMS-GlcNAc1/2+ ± Fuc to confirm core fucosylation. Additional criteria included expected retention times and elution order reported in the literature, as well as consistency with known biosynthetic pathways.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Aqueous stock solutions of the selected seven iRT peptides (LFLQFGAQGSPFLK, GTFIIDPGGVIR, YILAGVENSK, TPVITGAPYEYR, DGLDAASYYAPVR, ADVTPADFSEWSK, and VEATFGVDESNAK) were enriched with 0.001% PEG 20 000 and mixed to achieve similar concentrations of around 25 ng/μL.  Reconstituted therapeutic proteins were desalted and denatured at 2 µg/µL in 0.5% RapiGest SF prepared in 75 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, by incubation at 90 °C for 3 min. N-deglycosylation was performed using Rapid PNGase F at 50 °C for 5 min according to the manufacturer’s instructions, with 1.2 µL of enzyme stock added per 40 µg of protein. Released N-glycans were labeled using RapiFluor-MS labeling reagent at a final concentration of 20 μg/μL in 25% dimethyl formamide for 5 min at room temperature. The reaction mixture (40 µL) was diluted to 400 µL with acetonitrile (ACN) and loaded onto an in-house-prepared microSPE column packed with 5 mg of Spe-ed NH₂ aminopropyl sorbent in a Pierce Micro-Spin cartridge. The microSPE column was conditioned with water and equilibrated with 85% ACN, using 200 µL of each. After sample loading, glycans were washed with 1200 µL of 1% FA in 90% ACN and eluted with 90 µL of 200 mM ammonium acetate, pH 7, in 5% ACN. The SPE recovery was approximately 60%.  Reconstituted therapeutic proteins were denatured and reduced in 5 M guanidine hydrochloride containing 20 mM dithiothreitol at 37 °C for 30 min. Free thiol groups were blocked with 25 mM iodoacetamide for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. Proteins were subsequently desalted using Zeba spin columns and digested overnight at 37 °C with dimethylated SOLu-trypsin in 25% Low-Artifact Digestion Buffer at an enzyme-to-protein mass ratio of 1:50. Digestion was quenched by the addition of difluoroacetic acid, and the resulting digest was supplemented with 0.001% PEG 20 000.  For the LC-MS-related method description and treatment of prepared samples, see the manuscript.

Hyalectan Remodeling Contributes to Aortic Stenosis: Insights from Glycoproteomics
projectDescription: BACKGROUND: Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) is increasingly recognized as an active pathological process involving extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. This study investigates ECM remodeling through proteomic analysis and a novel mouse model of aortic stenosis (AS). METHODS: Proteomic and glycoproteomic analyses were conducted on aortic valve (AV) leaflets from heart transplant donors (n=29) and CAVD patients (n=17). Each CAVD sample was subdivided into non-calcified and calcified regions. To investigate the functional impact of ECM remodeling on AS, we crossed apolipoprotein E-deficient mice (ApoE-/-) with mice lacking the catalytic domain of ADAMTS5 (Adamts5Δcat) to generate a mouse model combining hyalectan accumulation with hypercholesterolemia. RESULTS: Proteomic and glycoproteomic analyses revealed hyalectan accumulation in CAVD compared to control valves. Versican predominated in non-calcified regions, while aggrecan was enriched in calcified regions. The shift in hyalectan composition correlated to changes in AV pressure gradient, elevated osteoblast-like cell markers, and inflammatory proteins, most notably pentraxin 3. Both versican and aggrecan are characterized by their ability to bind hyaluronan and serve as major substrates of ADAMTS5. In Adamts5Δcat/ApoE-/- mice, hyalectan accumulation was associated with a significant narrowed aortic cusps separation, and increased post AV velocity. Proteomic analysis of AVs from Adamts5Δcat/ApoE-/- mice revealed elevated versican, aggrecan, and pentraxin 3, recapitulating key features of human CAVD. Single-cell RNA sequencing and in vitro experiment linked versican to activated valve interstitial cells, while aggrecan co-localized with calcification markers in osteoblast-like cells. Pentraxin 3 was bound to hyaluronan and accumulated in calcified AVs. ADAMTS5 deficiency was sufficient to cause intact versican accumulation and promote valve interstitial cell differentiation, as evidenced by increased expression of osteopontin, which binds to hyaluronan receptors. CONCLUSIONS: This study highlights hyalectan remodelling during AS pathogenesis. A shift from versican to aggrecan in human CAVD correlates to changes in AV pressure gradient. In Adamts5Δcat/ApoE-/- mice, impaired hyalectan catabolism promotes AS.
dataProcessingProtocol: N-glycopeptide and O-glycopeptide were identified using Byonic (version 2.9.30, Proteome Metrics) with built-in N-glycan and O-glycan databases and a custom-made protein database (1526 protein entries) from the previous LC-MS/MS experiment using deglycosylated samples. To detect TMTpro-labelled peptides, the modifications specified in the quantification method (lysine and N-terminal residue modification + 304.2071 Da) were included in the search. The signal intensity of TMTpro reporter ions generated in HCD spectra were used as quantitation value of the peptides. Correction for the reagent lot-specific isotopic impurities of TMTpro tags was applied. To account for variation in abundance between samples, data was normalized to the total peptide amount. After normalization, protein abundance was scaled to the average abundance of the pooled sample.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The aortic valve (AV) leaflets from patients with calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD, n=15) were dissected into non-calcified and calcified areas. Together with AV leaflets from healthy donors (n=15), a total of 45 samples were used for glycoproteomics analysis. Diced human AV leaflets (40mg) were washed with PBS to remove the plasma contamination, incubated with 0.5M sodium chloride (NaCl) solution (0.5M NaCl, 10mM Tris, pH 7.5, 25mM EDTA, with proteinase inhibitors) on a shaker for 1 hour, followed by incubation with 4M guanidine hydrochloride (GuHCl) solution (4M GuHCl, 50mM sodium acetate, pH 5.8, 25mM EDTA, with proteinase inhibitors) for 48 hours. 35μg of protein from GuHCl extracts were precipitated with 100% ethanol (10x sample volume) at -20°C overnight and dried using a speed vacuum concentrator (Thermo Fisher Savant SpeedVac SPD131DDA). Dried protein pellets were resuspended in 6M urea, 2M thiourea, 0.1M TEAB (pH=8.5). After reduction with 10 mM dithiothreitol at 37°C for 1 hour, 240 rpm, the samples were cooled down to room temperature before being alkylated by 50 mM iodoacetamide in the dark for 1 hour. Prechilled (−20°C) acetone (8x sample volume) was used to precipitate the samples overnight at −20°C. Protein pellets were dried using SpeedVac, resuspended in 170 µL of 0.1 M TEAB (pH=8.2), and digested with trypsin/LysC (enzyme:protein=1:25) at 37°C overnight. The digestion was stopped with 1% TFA. The peptides were purified using C18 cartridges on a Bravo AssayMAP robot (Agilent) using the manufacturer’s protocol. The eluted peptides were dried using SpeedVac and resuspended in 35µL of 0.1M TEAB. Peptides were labelled using the TMTpro 16plex Isobaric Tandem Mass Tag Labeling Reagent Set (TMTpro), according to the manufacturer's instructions (Thermo Fisher Scientific). A pooled sample consisting of aliquots from all individual samples was used as a control and labelled with TMTpro-126. TMTpro-labelled peptides were further enriched for glycopeptides using zwitterionic hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (Agilent Poroshell 120 HILIC-Z 2.7um, 2.1mm x 100mm, PN 685775-924) and separated into 16 fractions. The glycopeptide enriched fraction was separated using the Vanquish Neo nanoflow liquid chromatography (LC) system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a C18 column (EASY-Spray, 50 cm×75 µm, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were eluted using 5% to 35% B (80% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid in H2O) within 70min at a flow rate of 300 nL/min and directly analyzed with an Orbitrap Ascend MS (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with electron transfer dissociation (ETD). The Orbitrap Ascend was operated in data-dependent acquisition mode where high resolution FT-MS scans (m/z 380-1500, resolution 120,000 (at m/z 200) and alternating ETD and HCD FT-MS2 scans (m/z 110-2000, resolution 45,000 (at m/z 200) were acquired. Precursor selection for MS2 includes: charge state 2-6, 40s dynamic exclusion window, intensity threshold 5e4 and quadrupole isolation width of 0.7m/z. Precursors meeting the criteria were prioritized based on highest charge state and most intense. The same precursor was fragmented by ETD and HCD within a 3s cycle time. ETD parameters include calibrated ETD reaction times and precursor AGC of 2e5 and 91ms max injection time. HCD parameters include 34 normalized collision energy and precursor AGC 2e4 and 91ms max injection time.

title: Relative Quantitative Analysis of Site-Specific N-Linked Glycosylation in Hyperglycosylated In-terferon-β via Mass Spectrometry
projectDescription: Glycosylation is a critical determinant of the efficacy, stability, and pharmacological behavior of therapeutic proteins. R27T, an engineered variant of interferon-β1a, contains two N-glycosylation sites (Asn25 and Asn80), increasing its structural complexity and analytical requirements. In this study, we performed comprehensive total and site-specific glycan profiling of R27T using complementary analytical approaches. For total glycan analysis, the released N-glycans were fluorescently labeled with procainamide, providing enhanced sensitivity and broader glycan coverage compared with conventional 2-aminobenzamide labeling. Site-specific glycan profiling was performed by LC–MS/MS–based peptide mapping. Protease digestion conditions were optimized to improve recovery of site-specific glycopeptides, with chymotryp-sin identified as the most effective enzyme for resolving glycopeptides from individual glyco-sylation sites. Total glycan distributions reconstructed from peptide-mapping data were com-pared with fluorescence-based glycan profiling, showing that total and site-specific glycan data can be effectively combined. Minor discrepancies were observed depending on glycan struc-ture, mainly due to differences in ionization efficiency. Distinct glycan distributions were iden-tified between the two N-glycosylation sites of R27T. Molecular modeling further suggested that the additional glycan at Asn25 may enhance structural stability and receptor-binding affini-ty. These results demonstrate an integrative strategy for accurate glycan characterization in mul-ti-site glycoproteins relevant to biotherapeutic development.
dataProcessingProtocol: N-linked Glycan Profiling Data analysis was performed using Byos software (version 5.3.44; Protein Metrics Inc.). Peptide Mapping Data processing was performed using the “N-glycan 309 mammalian no sodium” database from Protein Metrics. Glycoprotein-Receptor Complex Modeling with AlphaFold3  To investigate the structural and functional impact of the R27T-induced glycosylation site, two distinct models of the human IFN-β1 signaling complex were generated using AlphaFold3 (AF3). (41) Both models included the full-length extracellular domains of IFNAR1 (UniProt: P17181) and IFNAR2 (UniProt: P48551) receptors. The first model (Model 1, Control) consisted of wild-type IFN-β1 (N80-glycosylated) complexed with IFNAR1/IFNAR2.The second model (Model 2, R27T Variant) consisted of the engineered R27T variant (N25/N80-glycosylated) complexed with IFNAR1/IFNAR2. Structural modeling required precise specification of N-linked glycans, achieved by employing a hybrid input syntax combining Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD) codes with explicit “bondedAtomPairs” (BAP) definitions within the AF3 JSON input. (42) This advanced protocol ensures stereochemically, conformationally accurate models, as standard linear input formats can introduce ambiguities. The specific N-glycan structures modeled at each site were based on the most abundant glycoforms identified in our MS data. For the N80 site (present in both models), the A2G2FS1 glycan was modelled. For the N25 site (present only in Model 2), the highly complex A4G4FS2 + 1LacNAc glycan was modeled. The BAP syntax defines the precise covalent glycosidic linkages between monosaccharide units. For example, to link the first N-acetylglucosamine (NAG, CCD code) to the asparagine (Asn) residue, a bond was defined between the Asn Nδ2 atom and the NAG C1 atom. Subsequent linkages (e.g., the β(1,4) linkage between the first and second NAG residues) were defined by specifying a bond between the O4 atom of the first NAG and the C1 atom of the second NAG, following the protocol described by Huang et al. (2025). This protocol-driven approach ensures the generation of stereochemically valid static models for complex, branched glycans. Predictions were performed using the locally installed AF3 source code on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. The top-ranked model (Rank 0) based on the pLDDT and PAE (Predicted Aligned Error) confidence scores was selected for subsequent energy analysis.  Quantitative Binding Energy Calculation with EvoEF2 To quantify the differences in binding affinity, we employed the EvoEF2 energy function, a physics-based scoring function optimized for computational protein design and binding energy estimation. (43) EvoEF2 has high accuracy and computational speed. This workflow provides the quantitative binding energy data requested, expanding on the energy minimization step. First, the PDB files generated by AlphaFold3 (Model 1 and Model 2) were pre-processed. We used EvoEF2 to calculate the resulting protein-protein interaction energy, Itotal, of the specific, glycan-induced conformation. This allowed us to isolate the energetic contribution of the glycan-mediated conformational stabilization on the protein-protein interface. Protein PDB files were first optimized using the RepairStructure command of EvoEF2. This step reconstructs incomplete side chains and optimizes the hydrogen-bonding network. Then, the binding energy between the IFN-β variant and the IFNAR1/IFNAR2 receptor complex was calculated using the ComputeBinding command. The chains were split into two distinct interacting groups. Assuming IFN-β is chain A, IFNAR1 chain B, and IFNAR2 is chain C, the binding energy (∆Gbind) was computed as the difference between the total energy of the complex and those of the individual components (Chain A and Chain BC). The final Itotal value, which includes intra-chain van der Waals, electrostatic, hydrogen bonding, and solvation energy terms, is reported in kcal/mol. A more negative value indicates a more stable, higher-affinity interaction.
sampleProcessingProtocol: N-linked Glycan Profiling N-linked glycan profiles were analyzed using Ludger labeling kits (2-AB: LT-KAB-A2, Ludger, UK; procainamide: LT-KPROC-24, Ludger, UK). For protein denaturation and reduc-tion, 1 µL of 0.5 M dithiothreitol (DTT) (D5545; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) and 10 µL of 1% RapiGest SF (186001861; Waters, USA) were added to 0.2 mg of buffer-exchanged protein. The mixture was incubated at 65°C in a heat block for 30 min. After reaction completion, 2 µL of PNGase F (P0705L; NEB, USA) was added for enzymatic deglycosylation. The reaction products were then purified using an EB10 Cartridge (LC-EB10-A6; Ludger, UK), and the eluted glycans were collected and dried in a centrifugal evaporator. The dried glycan samples were labeled with either 2-AB or procainamide, depending on the experimental requirements. N-linked glycan analysis was performed using a Thermo Ultimate 3000 system coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion™ Tribrid™ mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, MA, USA) with an elec-trospray ionization (ESI) source. Separation of labeled glycans was achieved using an AC-QUITY UPLC Glycan BEH Amide Column (2.1 × 150 mm2, 1.7 μm; Waters, USA). Chro-matographic separation was performed at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min, with a column temperature of 60°C for 2-AB–labeled glycans and 40°C for procainamide-labeled glycans. Fluorescence detection was performed at excitation and emission wavelengths of 310 and 370 nm, respec-tively. The mass spectrometer was operated under the following ESI conditions: a sheath gas flow rate of 50 Arb, an auxiliary gas flow rate of 10 Arb, an ion transfer tube temperature of 325°C, and a vaporizer temperature of 350°C. For MS/MS analysis, the Orbitrap detector was configured with a resolution of 120,000 and a scan range of 600–2,500 m/z. The top 15 pre-cursor ions with the highest intensities were selected for MS/MS. Precursor ions exceeding a minimum intensity threshold of 1.0 × 104 were considered strong and dynamically excluded for 7 s following their detection. Precursor ions with charge states of 1–3 were chosen for MS/MS fragmentation. For glycan fragmentation in higher-energy collision (HCD) mode, stepped collision energy percentages were adjusted based on precursor m/z values and charge states to ensure optimal fragmentation. Peptide Mapping To perform site-specific glycan analysis of R27T via peptide mapping, the protein was digested using chymotrypsin, trypsin, and Glu-C. The aim was to determine which enzyme provided optimal site-specific glycan characterization. Glycopeptides from each digestion were analyzed via LC-MS using a C18 column, with identification conducted through MS/MS analysis using Byos software and XICs generated from the MS spectra. For sample preparation, 1 mg of R27T was treated with a denaturing buffer [7 M guanidine-HCl and 0.25 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.4)] containing 5 mM DTT (D5545; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) and incubated at 37°C for 60 min to fa-cilitate denaturation and reduction. Alkylation was performed by adding iodoacetamide (I4386; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) to a final concentration of 7.5 mM, followed by incubation in the dark at 25°C for 60 min. For enzymatic digestion, trypsin (11418025001; Roche, Switzerland) and chymotrypsin (11418467001; Roche, Switzerland) were added at a protein-to-enzyme ratio of 25:1 and incubated at 37°C for 18 h. Glu-C (11047817001; Roche, Switzerland) was used un-der the same ratio but incubated at 25°C for 18 h. Digested peptides were analyzed using the Thermo Ultimate 3000 system coupled to the Orbitrap Fusion™ Tribrid™ mass spectrometer with an ESI source (Thermo Scientific). Generated peptides were separated using an ACQUI-TY CSH C18 column (1.7 μm, 2.1 × 100 mm2; Waters, USA). MS analysis was conducted with the following parameters: a sheath gas flow of 50 Arb, an auxiliary gas flow of 10 Arb, an ion transfer temperature of 325°C, a vaporizer temperature of 350°C, spray voltage set to static, and a positive ion mode voltage of 3,500 V. MS/MS analysis was conducted using the Orbitrap detector with a resolution of 60,000, a scan range of 220–3,000, the RF lens set at 60%, an AGC target of 2.0 × 105, a maximum injection time of 50 ms, and microscans set to 1. Data analysis was conducted using Byos software (version 5.1.1; Protein Metrics Inc.) with a pre-cursor mass error tolerance of 20 ppm and a fragment mass error tolerance of 0.3 Da. Carbox-ymethylation was set as a common modification, whereas methionine oxidation and asparagine deamidation were considered rare modifications.

title: Glycoproteomics of Human and Mouse Brains in Alzheimer’s Disease
projectDescription: This study profiles glycoproteomic changes in human frontal cortex and mouse brain in Alzheimer’s disease models. We compare cognitively normal and AD human brain tissue, and wild-type and 5xFAD mouse brain, to define whether AD-associated hyperglycosylation reflects increased glycosylation of existing proteins. The work is integrated with spatial glycomics and related multiomic analyses to identify disease-associated glycopeptides and glycoproteins linked to neurodegeneration.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw glycoproteomics data were processed in Proteome Discoverer v3.0. Peptides were identified with CHIMERYS, and glycopeptides were assigned using the Byonic node. Search parameters included 5 ppm precursor tolerance and 10 ppm fragment tolerance. Variable modifications included deamidation, oxidation, and carboxymethylation. Glycopeptide identifications were filtered at log probability >1 and ppm error <3. Human samples were searched against the “N-glycan 182 human no multiple fucose” library, and mouse samples against the “N-glycan 309 mammalian no sodium” library. O-glycan searches used the “9-Most-common glycans” library. Curated outputs were used for relative glycopeptide quantification and downstream interpretation.
sampleProcessingProtocol: De-identified human frontal cortex specimens and mouse brain tissues were collected and prepared under approved protocols. For glycoproteomics, pooled samples were used to ensure sufficient membrane protein input. Membrane proteins were enriched by high-salt extraction, sodium carbonate fractionation, and sequential ultracentrifugation. The membrane fraction was denatured in urea buffer, reduced, alkylated with iodoacetamide, precipitated by chloroform/methanol/water extraction, and resuspended in ammonium bicarbonate. Protein concentration was measured by BCA assay, and 100 µg of membrane protein was digested with trypsin at 37°C for 24 h. Glycopeptides were then analyzed by nanoLC on an Ultimate 3000 RSLCnano coupled to a Thermo Eclipse mass spectrometer using a 15 cm × 75 µm C18 column and a 180 min gradient.

title: Mouse tissue glycoproteome atlas
projectDescription: Sex-specific glycoproteome differences remain poorly understood despite emerging evidence pointing to protein glycosylation being a principal contributor to sex biology. Here, we present a comprehensive, tissue-resolved glycoproteome atlas of adult male and female C57BL/6N mice, integrating comparative transcriptomics, proteomics and glycoproteomics with sialic acid speciation and lectin microarray analyses across 19 mouse tissues. Quantitative profiling of >26,800 protein- and site-specific N-glycoforms covering 1,512 glycoproteins revealed that each tissue exhibits a distinct glycoproteome shaped by unique proteome and glycosylation traits. The tissue glycome diversity was governed by coordinated regulation of glyco-enzymes and protein expression patterns. Amongst many other glycophenotype-enzyme associations, multi-omics data integration indicated that tissue sialylation is governed by Cmas and Cmah suggesting that these are rate-limiting biosynthetic enzymes in the glycosylation machinery. Notably, we found that the salivary gland, liver, and kidney display pronounced sex-linked glycophenotypes driven by profound differences of fucosylation, sialylation and global protein levels in male and female mice. In contrast, the brain displayed extensive glycome diversity that was largely conserved between males and females, highlighting constraints within sex-specific glycosylation. An online database provides an interactive resource for exploring new molecular facets of sex-biased biology through the sex-linked glycoproteome variations that exist across mouse tissues.
dataProcessingProtocol: Glycoproteomics and proteomics data processing and analysis For glycoproteomics, HCD-MS/MS data were searched with Byonic (v2.6.46, Protein Metrics) using 10/20 ppm as the precursor/product ion mass tolerance, respectively. Cys carbamidomethylation (+57.021 Da) and N-term/Lys TMT (+229.163 Da) were considered fixed modifications. Fully tryptic peptides were searched with up to two missed cleavages per peptide. For the variable modifications, up to two common and one rare modification(s) were permitted per peptide. Methionine oxidation (+15.994 Da) was defined as a common modification, while N-glycosylation of sequon-localized asparagine residues was specified as a rare modification. The N-glycan search space comprised 309 predefined mammalian structures available in Byonic (excluding sodium adducts) manually supplemented with an additional 151 glycomics-informed entries from a recent high-quality N-glycome map of mouse tissues12 for a total glycan search space of 460 glycan compositions. The HCD-MS/MS data were searched against the UniProt Reference Mus musculus proteome (17,150 reviewed sequences, UniProtKB, released June 2023). All searches were filtered to <1% false discovery rate (FDR) at the glycoprotein and glycopeptide level using a protein decoy database. Only confident glycopeptide identifications (PEP 2D < 0.01) were considered. Glycopeptides were quantified using the ‘Report Ion Quantifier’ available as a node in Proteome Discoverer (v2.2, Thermo)45. Glycopeptides were manually grouped by summing the reporter ion intensities from the glycopeptide-to-spectrum matches (glycoPSMs) belonging to the same UniProtKB identifier, same glycosylation site within each protein, and same glycan composition. Within each sample, the total set of glycopeptide forms from each glycosylation site from each protein were normalized to 100%. For proteomics, HCD-MS/MS data (from both unenriched and HILIC flow-through fractions) were processed using Proteome Discoverer v3.0 and searched against UniProt Reference Mus musculus proteome (17,150 reviewed sequences, UniProtKB, released June 2023) using the Sequest-HT search engine with a mass tolerance of 5 ppm for precursor ions and 10 ppm for product ions. The enzyme specificity was set to trypsin with a maximum of two missed cleavages permitted. Carbamidomethylation of Cys (+57.021 Da) and N-term/Lys TMT (+229.163 Da) were fixed modifications whereas Met oxidation (+15.994 Da) was a variable modification. Both protein and peptide level identifications were filtered to 1% FDR. The TMT-based protein abundances were normalized by ratio to the reference channel and total peptide as previously described.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Tissue and blood collection Whole blood was collected into EDTA-coated tubes from the right atrium immediately after sacrifice. Plasma was separated by centrifugation (200 × g, 20 min, 4°C) and stored at −80°C. The following tissues were surgically excised by a trained animal technician and snap-frozen at −80°C: brain (whole), eyes, salivary gland, thymus, heart, lung, liver, stomach, pancreas, spleen, small intestine, kidney, urinary bladder, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, and skin. Sex-specific organs were also collected (testes from males; ovaries from females). All samples were stored at −80°C until processing.  Protein extraction and digestion Frozen tissues were lysed in 500 µL RIPA buffer (PBS, 1% Triton X-100, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM PMSF, 10 mM NaF, 1 mM sodium orthovanadate, protease inhibitor cocktail) and homogenized using 3 mm zirconium beads in a TissueLyser (30 Hz, 2 min). Protein concentrations were determined by BCA assay. Proteins were precipitated with four volumes of acetone (16 h, −30°C), pelleted (14,000 rpm, 10 min, 4°C), and resuspended in 8 M urea in 50 mM TEAB.  Proteins were reduced (10 mM DTT, 30 min, 30°C), alkylated (40 mM iodoacetamide, 30 min, dark, 20°C), and quenched with excess DTT. Samples were digested with sequencing-grade trypsin (1:50 w/w, 12 h, 37°C). Digestion was stopped with 1% TFA. Peptides were desalted using Oligo R3 reversed-phase SPE microcolumns and dried.  TMT labelling and experimental design Peptides were labelled with TMT reagents following the manufacturer’s protocol. For each tissue, peptides from 20 µg protein extracts of five male and five female mice were labelled using TMT11plex reagents. A pooled peptide reference (2 µg from each sample) was included in each TMT-10/11plex set to enable cross-experiment normalization, consistently assigned to the 131C reporter channel.  Peptides were dissolved in 100 mM TEAB and labelled (1 h, 20°C), and reactions were quenched with 5% hydroxylamine (15 min). Labelled samples were mixed 1:1 (w/w) and desalted using hydrophilic–lipophilic balance SPE cartridges. An aliquot (10 µg) was reserved for direct LC-MS/MS analysis (unenriched proteome fraction). The remaining peptides were dried for glycopeptide enrichment.  Glycopeptide enrichment Approximately 220 µg of TMT-labelled peptides were reconstituted in 80% ACN/1% TFA and loaded onto custom ZIC-HILIC SPE microcolumns packed with zwitterionic resin. Flow-through and wash fractions (non-glycosylated peptides) were retained for proteome analysis. Glycopeptides were sequentially eluted with 0.1% TFA, 25 mM ammonium bicarbonate, and 50% ACN, pooled, desalted (Oligo R3 SPE), aliquoted, and dried. Enriched glycopeptide and unenriched peptide fractions were analyzed separately.  LC-MS/MS analysis Samples were analyzed on a Vanquish Neo UHPLC coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 240 mass spectrometer operating in positive ion mode. Peptides were trapped on a PepMap Neo nano trap cartridge and separated on a 25 cm Aurora Ultimate analytical column at 300 nL/min. The gradient was 3–35% solvent B (90 min), 35–50% B (8 min), 50–90% B (2 min), followed by 10 min at 95% B (solvent A: 0.1% FA; solvent B: 99.9% ACN/0.1% FA).  For enriched glycopeptides, MS1 scans were acquired at 120,000 resolution (m/z 500–2,000, 100 ms max injection time). Data-dependent acquisition (3 s cycle time) selected multiply charged precursors (z ≥ 2) for stepped HCD fragmentation (NCE 20/30/40%). MS2 spectra were acquired at 45,000 resolution with a 1.6 m/z isolation window and 20 s dynamic exclusion.  For unenriched peptide fractions, MS1 scans were acquired at 120,000 resolution (m/z 380–1,800). Data-dependent HCD-MS/MS (NCE 30%) was performed with a 1.4 m/z isolation window, 45,000 resolution MS2 scans, and 20 s dynamic exclusion.  This workflow enabled parallel quantitative proteome and site-specific N-glycoproteome profiling across multiple tissues from male and female mice using TMT-based multiplexing combined with HILIC enrichment and high-resolution Orbitrap LC-MS/MS analysis.

title: Site-Specific Glycosylation Profiling of Protein Subunit and Inactivated Virus Vaccines
projectDescription: Many protein subunit vaccines and biologics contain glycosylated antigens and antibodies, yet quantitative frameworks for comparing glycosylation across lots, manufacturers, and production platforms remain limited. We performed site specific glycosylation LC-MS/MS analysis for intact N-linked glycopeptides on licensed protein subunit vaccines, including influenza from egg-, MDCK-, and Sf9-derived products, plus Sf9 SARS-CoV-2 spike and CHO varicella-zoster virus glycoprotein E. Glycopeptide abundance distribution spectra were compared using the NIST MS Search dot-product score to quantify similarity of site-specific glycan distributions. Across all sites, distributions clustered into six recurrent classes (two high-mannose, three core-fucosylated complex, and one multi-sialylated complex profile). Replicate analyses, year-to-year formulations, and different manufacturers within the same platform were highly similar (scores 978, 961, and 960 out of 999), whereas intra-protein sites, influenza inter-strain sites, and different production sources were less similar (scores 554, 540, and 209). Interestingly, glycosylation differences between production sources tracked phylogenetic relatedness of host species.
dataProcessingProtocol: Glycopeptide identifications and abundances were primarily derived from MSFragger software output (version 4.1).46, 47 Search parameters included three maximum missed cleavages, with six maximum missed cleavages for alpha-lytic protease, a precursor mass tolerance of 10 ppm, and fragment mass error of 20 ppm. Cysteine carbamidomethylation (+57.02) was set as a fixed modification and variable modifications included methionine oxidation (+15.99) and glutamine N-terminal ammonia loss (-17.03). The glycan database used for searching consists of 444 human N-glycans and is composed of glycans found in mammalian, human, and sulfation databases48. Within the data processing pipeline, FDR was not used for validation of glycopeptide MS2 spectra since it does not consider multiple factors used in the present validation scheme such as retention time, presence of oxonium ions and consistency of HCD and ion trap spectra.  As reported previously3, annotated tandem glycopeptide libraries were created using a suite of in-house software which includes MS_Piano49 for the annotation of tandem spectra for N-glycopeptides. MS_Piano annotates both peptides and intact N-glycopeptides by sequence, charge state, and modification. Spectra shown in the paper employed this annotation. The suite of software used for tandem library creation begins with output data from MSFragger which tentatively identifies glycopeptides and provides XIC (extracted ion chromatogram) information from MS1 data. Identified glycopeptides are then subject to further validation based on contingent ion-trap collision-induced dissociation (CID) fragmentation spectra, retention time, Y ion presence, purity, XIC overlap, and number of identified HCD spectra found. The annotated and validated glycopeptide spectra are then converted into NIST MS library format. Two different, well identified glycopeptides were required for GADS generation. Resulting GADS libraries can be visualized, compared, and searched within the NIST MS Search software 50. Glycopeptide Abundance Distribution Spectra (GADS) were created for each digest as a means of storing glycosylation distributions. Each GADS represents many glycoforms for one peptide sequence from one sample injection into the mass spectrometer. Briefly, these pseudo-spectra were created from MS2 glycopeptide spectra with glycan mass as the x-axis and their MS1 XIC abundances on the y-axis. Each GADS peak represents a glycan with monosaccharides represented as follows: G represents HexNac (N-acetylhexosamine), H represents hexose, F represents fucose (deoxyhexose), S represents sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid), and Po represents phosphorylation.24 No sulfation (So) was confidently detected. Red peaks represent less confident glycopeptide identifications that may have several origins, including inconsistent retention time, lack of a Y1 ion, lack of expected oxonium ions and other factors. GADS represent all glycopeptides from a single sequence and charge state for a single run, enabling direct comparison between glycan distributions between repeat runs for a given sequence. As discussed previously, multiple charge state GADS were constructed when or more individual charge state GADS were generated for a single sequence.24 In-house software was used to create GADS pseudo-spectra from MSfragger output and from validation information from the in-house tandem mass spectral library creation software.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Methods of protein digestion and sample cleanup are derived from previous work and are recapitulated here. Two methods of protein digestion were used in this work. The first is an in-solution method, which was used for vaccines that did not contain adjuvants or amphipathic additives such as Tween-20 or Triton X-100. The in-solution method was adapted from Cyr et al39. In summary, each sample contained 10 µg of estimated protein and was diluted to 1 mL using 50 mmol/L ammonium bicarbonate (ABC) and subsequently dialyzed in a Spectra/Por® 7 dialysis membrane with 1000 Da molecular weight cutoff (Avantor). Dialysis was performed in a 1 L reagent bottle with 10 mmol/L ABC as the dialysate. The bottle was placed in an ice bath with stirring. The first two rounds of dialysis were conducted for 2 h each and the third round of dialysis was conducted overnight. After dialysis, the samples were then dried down using a Genevac EZ-2 plus Speedvac (SP Scientific) using Aqueous mode at 40 °C for 1 h or until dry. Samples were then reconstituted in 50 µL of purified water from a Milli-Q system. Dithiothreitol was then added to reach a final concentration of 20 mmol/L. The solution was left to incubate at 60 °C for 1 h in an Eppendorf thermomixer at 450 rpm. After reduction, the reaction tube was cooled to room temperature and iodoacetamide added to reach a concentration of 55 mmol/L. The tube was again left to incubate at room temperature for 45 min in an Eppendorf thermomixer at 450 rpm with a covered cap. After cysteine alkylation, the sample was dialyzed, dried down, and reconstituted as described previously.  The second method of digestion used in-gel techniques adapted from previous work41, 42. This method of protein digestion was performed on vaccines which contained adjuvants or strong surfactants. Buffer exchange and protein gel electrophoresis were conducted as follows. 20 µg of estimated protein was buffer exchanged for each sample using a 0.5 mL 3K centrifugal filter (Amicon) and spun at 14,000 x g for 30 min. 400uL of 25 mmol/L ABC was added to the filter and the device was again spun at 14,000 x g for 30 min. The filter was then deposited upside-down in a new tube and spun at 1,000 x g for 2 min. 100 µL of 25 mmol/L ABC was added to the filter membrane and repeatedly pipetted in and out for agitation, with care as to not touch the membrane. The filter was again deposited upside-down in the tube and spun at 1,000 x g for 2 min. This process was completed two more times for a total of ~300 µL of protein concentrate. After buffer exchange, each sample was dried down using the Genevac EZ-2 plus Speedvac in Aqueous mode at 40 °C for about 1 h or until dry. Each sample was then reconstituted in 13 µL of Milli-Q water. The protocol was then followed from NuPAGE™ Bis-Tris mini gels (ThermoFisher).43      In-gel digestion of vaccine proteins started with gel destaining. Gel pieces were destained with 150 µL of 25 mmol/L ABC / 50% acetonitrile (ACN) (v/v) for 10 min. Destaining was performed two more times. Gel pieces were then dried down in the speedvac for 30 minutes or until gel pieces were white. Gel pieces were then rehydrated with 150 µL of 20 mmol/L DTT and incubated at 60 °C for 1 h at 450 rpm. After reduction, excess liquid was removed from the gel pieces and 150 µL of 55 mmol/L IAA was added to each sample. Alkylation proceeded with incubation at room temperature for 45 min at 450 rpm in the dark. After alkylation, excess liquid was removed from the gel pieces and 150 µL of 25 mmol/L ABC was added to the tube to rinse the gel pieces for 10 min. Supernatant was removed and the gel pieces were then dehydrated with 150 µL of 25 mmol/L ABC / 50% ACN (v/v) and let sit for 10 minutes. The supernatant was removed and the dehydration was repeated two more times. The samples were then dried down using a speedvac for 30 minutes or until gel pieces were white. Gel pieces were then rehydrated on ice using 150 µL of different chilled protease solutions. Protease combinations were as previously described for the in-solution digestion. Samples were left on ice for 30 minutes for rehydration in the protease solution and then excess liquid was removed. Gel pieces were then quickly rinsed with 50 µL of 25 mmol/L ABC. Durations and temperatures of digestion were as previously described for the in-solution digestions. After digestion, peptide extraction was completed using 75 µL of 50% ACN / 5% formic acid (FA) (v/v) with a 30 min incubation at room temperature followed by 5 min of sonication in a bath sonicator (bath sonicator info). Extraction using 50% ACN / 5% FA (v/v) was completed twice and extraction using 50% isopropanol / 5% FA (v/v) was completed once. After extraction, the resulting pool extract was dried down in a speedvac for 1 h and reconstituted in 0.1% TFA (v/v) for monospin purification. All digests were desalted using MonoSpin C18 SPE spin centrifuge columns (GL sciences).

title: Glycoproteomic and genetic analysis of N-glycosylation of complement component C3 reveals immune pathway regulation
projectDescription: This dataset comprises site-specific glycopeptide analysis of complement component C3 from plasma samples of 816 adults from the Korčula cohort (Croatia). C3 glycopeptides were enriched using Concanavalin A lectin affinity chromatography and analyzed by nano-LC-MS/MS. The study characterizes the N-glycan repertoire at both occupied glycosylation sites (N63 and N917), which carry exclusively high-mannose structures including unusual monoglucosylated glycoforms (Glc1Man9GlcNAc2, Glc1Man8GlcNAc2). Glycopeptide quantification was performed to assess associations with demographic and biochemical traits, and to conduct genome-wide association analysis identifying genetic determinants of C3 glycosylation. This represents the first large-scale population-level analysis of site-specific C3 N-glycosylation.
dataProcessingProtocol: Glycopeptide analysis was performed using an ACQUITY H-class UPLC system (Waters) coupled to a Synapt G2-Si ESI-QTOF mass spectrometer (Waters). Separation was achieved on an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 column (130Å, 1.7 µm, 1 mm × 150 mm) at 30°C with a linear gradient of 12-19% acetonitrile containing 0.1% formic acid over 16 minutes at 0.4 ml/min. Mass spectra were acquired in positive ion mode (500-2500 m/z). Data files were converted to mzXML using ProteoWizard MSConvert and processed using LaCyTools (version 1.0.1) for automated relative quantification of glycopeptides. Quality control included mass accuracy (<30 ppm), isotopic pattern quality (<25%), and signal-to-noise ratio (>15). Batch correction was performed using the ComBat method.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Plasma samples were collected from fasting participants from the island of Korčula (Croatia) and stored at -80°C until analysis. Complement component C3 was enriched from 10 μl human plasma using Concanavalin A (ConA)-Sepharose 4B (Global Life Sciences Solutions) lectin affinity chromatography. Plasma samples were diluted in binding buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, 0.5 M NaCl, 1 mM MnCl₂, 1 mM CaCl₂, pH 7.4) and incubated with conditioned ConA resin for 2 h at 4°C. After washing with binding buffer, bound glycoproteins were eluted with 200 mM methyl α-D-mannopyranoside in 0.1 M acetic acid (pH 3.0). Eluates were dried using a SpeedVac Vacuum Concentrator and resuspended in 15% (v/v) 2-propanol in 0.1 M ammonium acetate, followed by denaturation at 60°C for 10 min. Samples were digested with endoproteinase Glu-C (Sigma-Aldrich) at 1:50 enzyme:protein ratio (w/w) for 18 h at 37°C. Glycopeptides were enriched using Chromabond HILIC silica beads (Macherey-Nagel) with 0.1% TFA in 85% acetonitrile as binding buffer, washed, and eluted with 0.1% TFA.
