title: Expanding glycopeptide identification with Match-Between-Glycans (MBG) in FragPipe
projectDescription: Glycosylation is one of the most important, but also most complex, post-translational modifications of proteins. Mass spectrometry-based glycoproteomics analysis offers a powerful approach to explore the fundamental roles of glycosylation, but achieving sufficient fragmentation for glycopeptide assignment remains challenging, especially for low-abundant glycopeptides and large, complex glycans. We introduce match-between-glycans (MBG), a lightweight, modular MS1-based method integrated into the FragPipe computational platform that expands glycopeptide identification by leveraging learned retention time (RT) and ion mobility (IM) shifts between glycan compositions. MBG can also identify glycans not included in the glycan database, such as those containing adducts or modifications, without expanding the search space. This submission includes original human plasma PASEF data (6 technical replicates, timsTOF HT) and re-analysis results from four publicly available datasets: fission yeast (PXD005565), mouse liver (PXD005553), mouse brain (PXD005411), and CPTAC glioblastoma (GBM, from the Proteomic Data Commons at https://pdc.cancer.gov/). MBG expanded glycopeptide identifications across all datasets, including 14.6% more in human plasma, and enabled detection of glycopeptide adducts (NH4+, Fe3+, Na+) and mannose-6-phosphate glycans.
dataProcessingProtocol: All datasets were analyzed using FragPipe with MSFragger-Glyco, IonQuant, Philosopher, PTM-Shepherd, and Match-Between-Glycans (MBG). Common search parameters across all datasets: trypsin digestion with up to two missed cleavages; variable modifications of methionine oxidation and protein N-terminal acetylation; N-glycan mode; precursor and fragment mass tolerances of 20 ppm and 10 ppm; isotope error correction enabled; ion types b, y, b+HexNAc, y+HexNAc, and Y; oxonium ion filtering with minimum 10% relative intensity. PSM probabilities were modeled using PeptideProphet in semi-parametric mode with extended mass model (mass width: 4000), N-glycan motif modeling enabled, and cLevel = 0. Protein inference was performed with ProteinProphet (maxppmdiff = 20,000,000). FDR thresholds were 1% at PSM, ion, peptide, and protein levels. PTM-Shepherd was used for glycan assignment and glycan FDR filtering. Common MBG parameters: maximum glycan shift steps = 2, maximum q-values = 0.01, minimum glycans per site = 2, minimum PSMs = 1, RT tolerance = 0.4 min, m/z tolerance = 10 ppm. Dataset-specific settings: (1) Fission yeast: Searched against a yeast proteome database (downloaded 07/02/2025, 5,236 non-decoy entries). Glycan database: yeast and mouse combined with 1,701 entries (including high-mannose glycans from HexNAc(2)Hex(3) to HexNAc(2)Hex(20)), totaling 2,315 unique glycan masses with one NH4 adduct allowed per glycan. MBG FDR = 0.01 and 0.05. Glycan composition shifts: Hex(1), NH4(1) (normal search); Hex(1), NH4(1), NeuAc(1), HexNAc(1)Hex(1)NeuAc(1) (entrapment search). (2) Human plasma PASEF: Searched against a human proteome database (downloaded 07/02/2025, 20,453 non-decoy entries). Glycan database: "Human N-glycans medium-253" (506 glycans with one NH4 adduct allowed per glycan). "IM-MS" selected as MS data type. MBG glycan composition shifts: HexNAc, Hex, Fuc, NH4, NeuAc, HexNAc(1)Hex(1)NeuAc(1), HexNAc(1)Hex(1). (3) CPTAC GBM: Searched against the same protein database as the CPTAC GBM paper (Liu et al., Cancer Cell, 2024), with a glycan database excluding adducts. Searched using the "glyco-N-TMT" workflow with TMT-11 label type. MBG glycan composition shifts: HexNAc, Hex, Fuc, NeuAc, HexNAc(1)Hex(1)NeuAc(1), HexNAc(1)Hex(1). (4) Mouse liver: Searched against a mouse proteome database (downloaded 07/03/2025, 17,352 non-decoy entries). Same glycan database as the yeast search. MBG glycan composition shifts: HexNAc, Hex, Fuc, NeuAc, HexNAc(1)Hex(1)NeuAc(1), HexNAc(1)Hex(1), Fe, Na, NH4. (5) Mouse brain: Searched against the same mouse proteome database as mouse liver. A small glycan database with 196 entries including 14 phospho-glycans was used for mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) glycan search. MBG glycan composition shifts: HexNAc, Hex, Fuc, HexNAc(1)Hex(1), Phospho, NH4.
sampleProcessingProtocol: This submission contains one original dataset and re-analysis results from four public datasets: (1) Human plasma PASEF (original data): Human pooled plasma samples (VisuCon-F Normal Donor Set, EFNCP0125, Affinity Biologicals) were denatured, reduced, and alkylated using SDC, TCEP, and CAA, followed by overnight digestion with trypsin and Lys-C. Peptides were desalted using Oasis PRiME HLB (10 mg) 96-well plates (Waters) and glycopeptides were enriched using cotton-HILIC with 10 mm cotton thread on in-house made SPE tips (6 technical replicates). Samples were dried and resuspended in 0.1% TFA. LC-MS/MS analysis was performed on a timsTOF HT mass spectrometer (Bruker) coupled to an Ultimate3000 UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Glycopeptides were separated on an Aurora Ultimate XT column (25 cm × 75 µm, C18) at 50 °C with a 400 nL/min flow rate using a linear gradient from 3% to 35.2% buffer B (0.1% FA in ACN) over 130 min (buffer A: 0.1% FA in water). The timsTOF HT was operated in positive mode (100–1700 m/z, TIMS range 0.5–1.6 Vs/cm²) with 7 PASEF ramps, charge range 2–5, and stepped collision energy (35/40 eV at 0.50 Vs/cm² and 65/100 eV at 1.6 Vs/cm²). title: Truncated N-glycans destabilize POMT1 and POMT2 but do not limit cellular O-mannosylation in HEK293 cells
projectDescription: Protein O-mannosylation is initiated by the ER-resident enzymes POMT1 and POMT2, both of which carry multiple N-glycans essential for proper folding and activity. Although congenital disorders of glycosylation type I (CDG-I) disrupt the early N-glycosylation process, their impact on POMT biogenesis and O-mannosylation has remained unclear. Here, we show that ALG3-dependent N-glycan elongation is required to maintain normal abundance of POMT1 and POMT2. In ALG3-deficient HEK293 cells, POMTs carry truncated Man5 type N glycans and their steady-state protein levels are reduced by more than half, despite unchanged transcript levels. In vitro, reduced POMT abundance resulted in a proportional decrease in mannosyltransferase activity. However, O-mannosylation in cells remained unaffected: α-dystroglycan displayed normal matriglycan extension and a highly O mannosylated KIAA1549 reporter showed unaltered site occupancy and core structures. These data indicate that POMT activity operates with substantial catalytic reserve under basal conditions, sufficient to tolerate significant reduction in enzyme levels without impairing substrate modification. Our work identifies ALG3-mediated N-glycan maturation as a determinant of POMT stability, highlights buffering capacity within the O-mannosylation pathway, and provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how N-glycosylation defects could modulate POMT dependent glycosylation in disease.

Each sample was separately digested with Trypsin, Chymotrypsin or GluC. Protease digests were analyzed by bottom-up MS/MS on Fusion Orbitrap (HCD/ETciD, 60 min gradient).

Molecular characterization of patient-derived Follicular Lymphoma and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia B cell receptor variable domain glycans
projectDescription: Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a systemic, lymphoid tissue-derived neoplasm of germinal center phenotype B cells that have undergone a t(14;18) chromosomal translocation. A remarkable feature of B cell receptors (BCRs) expressed by FL B cells is the presence of variable domain N-linked glycosylation sites, which are introduced during a process called somatic hypermutation. These novel glycosylation sites are preferentially located in specific ‘hotspot’ sites and are suggested to play a role in the survival of FL B cells, feasibly via the interactions between the N-glycans that occupy these sites and environmental lectins. Thus far, in-depth, molecular characterization of patient-derived, primary FL BCR variable domain glycans (VDGs) has not been performed. In this report, using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, we assess the glycosylation profiles of 14 VDG sites from 9 unique patient-derived tumors, and as a comparator, include 3 patient-derived chronic lymphocytic leukemia B cell clones, each harboring a VDG site. We show that FL BCR heavy chain VDG are enriched in oligomannose-type glycans and show using molecular dynamics simulations, that the level of glycan processing correlates with the accessibility of glycosidase ERManI to the glycosylation site and is additionally affected by steric hindrance from neighboring glycans.
dataProcessingProtocol: In a post-analysis process, Byonic V5.7.11 (Protein Metrics) was used with 10 ppm and 20 ppm deviation for precursor and fragment mass, respectively, and no enzyme was specified (1). Oxidation on methionine and acetylation on the N-terminus were set as a “common” modification; carbamidomethyl on cysteine was set as a “fixed” modification. N-glycan modification was set to “rare”. LC-MS data was further quantified using Skyline (V22.2.0.527, ProteoWizard). The identified glycopeptides and complete list of identified compositions were imported into Skyline. Extracted ion chromatograms were generated for the first three isotopologues of each glycan. Glycopeptide-glycan combinations were validated based on isotopic pattern (idotp), mass accuracy, and retention time. Next, MS/MS analysis was used to validate peptide-glycan combinations at glycosylation sites. Next, quantification of the analytes was done by integrating the MS1 isotopologue peaks and summing the charge states. Relative quantification of glycoforms per glycopeptide was done in Microsoft Excel by normalizing the intensity per glycoform to the total area intensity. Relative abundances of all identified N-glycans per glycopeptide can be found in Supplementary Table 3 and tandem-MS verification can be found in Supplemental Data 1.
sampleProcessingProtocol: For MS analysis, gel bands were reduced with 10 mM dithiothreitol, and alkylated with 50 mM iodoacetamide. In-gel trypsin digestion was performed using a Proteineer DP digestion robot (Bruker). Tryptic peptides were extracted from the gel slices using 50/50/0.1 water/acetonitrile/formic acid (v/v/v). Samples were then lyophilized and endo Glu-C was added for a two-step digestion. The samples were lyophilized again, dissolved in water/formic acid (100/0.1 v/v) and analyzed by on‐line C18 nanoHPLC MS/MS with a system consisting of an Ultimate3000nano gradient HPLC system (Thermo Fisher, Bremen, Germany), and an Exploris480 mass spectrometer (Thermo). Peptides were injected onto a cartridge precolumn (300 μm × 5 mm, C18 PepMap, 5 um, 100 A, and eluted via a homemade analytical nano-HPLC column (50 cm × 75 μm; Reprosil-Pur C18-AQ 1.9 um, 120 A (Dr. Maisch, Ammerbuch, Germany). The gradient was run from 2% to 40% solvent B (20/80/0.1 water/acetonitrile/formic acid (FA) v/v) in 30 min. The nano-HPLC column was drawn to a tip of ∼10 μm and acted as the electrospray needle of the MS source. The mass spectrometer was operated in data-dependent Top 20 MS/MS mode, with a HCD collision energy at 30% and recording of the MS2 spectrum in the orbitrap, with a quadrupole isolation width of 1.2 Da. In the master scan (MS1) the resolution was 120,000, the scan range 400-3500, at standard AGC target @maximum fill time of 50 ms. A lock mass correction on the background ion m/z=445.12003 was used. Precursors were dynamically excluded after n=1 with an exclusion duration of 10 s, and with a precursor range of 20 ppm. Charge states 1-7 were included. For MS2 the first mass was set to 110 Da, and the MS2 scan resolution was 30,000 at an AGC target of 100% @maximum fill time of 60 ms. An additional MS2 scan was triggered if the HexNAc oxonium ion 204.087 was present in an MS2 spectrum. The same precursor was again selected, now with a stepped collision energy of 20, 35 and 50%, the maximum fill time was adjusted to 200 ms at a normalized AGC target of 500%, a mass resolution of 30,000 and a mass range of 110-3500.

title: Functional assays of human ALG9
projectDescription: Asparagine-linked glycans are essential for the maturation and function of most eukaryotic secretory proteins. Biosynthesis and transfer of the GlcNAc2Man9Glc3 glycan occurs on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane, in a highly conserved process involving more than a dozen membrane proteins whose dysfunction is linked to severe congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDGs). Three membrane-integral mannosyltransferases ALG3, ALG9 and ALG12 mediate four consecutive mannosylation reactions that convert GlcNAc2Man5 to GlcNAc2Man9. Using chemo-enzymatically synthesised lipid-linked glycan donor and acceptor analogues, we recapitulated this biosynthetic pathway in vitro. High-resolution cryo-EM structures of pseudo-Michaelis complexes of each step revealed the molecular basis of how the branched glycan is accurately synthesised in sequential reactions. Molecular dynamics simulations, mutagenesis, and functional assays uncovered a subtle but high precision mechanisms selecting the dolichylphosphomannose donor substrate over the also present epimer, dolichylphosphoglucose. Together, our results provide mechanistic explanations for enzyme disfunction in CDG and offer opportunities for N-glycan engineering.
dataProcessingProtocol: The mass spectrometer was operated under data-dependent acquisition (DDA), one scan cycle comprised of a full scan MS survey spectrum, followed by up to 12 sequential HCD MS/MS on the most intense signals above a threshold of 1e4. Full-scan MS spectra (300–1800 m/z) were acquired in the FT-Orbitrap at a resolution of 120,000 at 400 m/z, while HCD MS/MS spectra were recorded in the FT-Orbitrap at a resolution of 60,000 at 400 m/z. HCD was performed with a target value of 1e5 and normalization collision energy 32 was applied. AGC target values were 5e5 for full FTMS. For all experiments, dynamic exclusion was used with a single repeat count, 15 s repeat duration, and 30 s exclusion duration.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Activity assays with human ALG9 were performed with 100 nM wildtype or enzyme variant, 10 µM acceptor substrate and 20 µM donor substrate. Reactions were carried out at room temperature in reaction buffer (150 mM sodium chloride, 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 0.01 % LMNG and 0.001 % CHS) for 30 seconds before being heated to 95ºC for 10 minutes unless otherwise noted. The resulting lipid-linked oligosaccharide samples were then transferred to a peptide fluorescently labelled with carboxytetramethylrhodamine (TAMRA) using TbSTT3B. The peptide had the sequence: TAMRA-YANATS-NH2 (Genscript). Briefly, 200 nM TbSTT3B was incubated with 5 µM LLO and 10 µM peptide in transfer buffer (150 mM sodium chloride, 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 10 mM MnCl2, 0.035 % DDM and 0.007 % CHS) at 30ºC for at least 4 hours. LC-MS/MS glycopeptide analysis was performed at the Functional Genomics Center Zurich. The samples were diluted 20 times with 0.1% formic acid before injection of 2 µL on a calibrated Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fischer Scientific) coupled to a nano-Acquity UPLC system (Waters). Peptides were loaded onto a nanoEase M/Z Symmetry C18, Trap Column (180 µm x 20 mm, 100 Å, 5 μm particle size) and separated on a nanoEase M/Z HSS C18 T3 (75 μm × 150 mm, 100 Å, 1.8 μm particle size), at a constant flow rate of 300 nL min-1, with a column temperature of 50 °C and a linear gradient of 2−35% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid in 20 min, and then 35-98% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid in 5 min, and then held isocratically for another 5 min.

title: Parallel Reaction Monitoring to Assess High-Affinity N-Glycoforms of the Human Fcγ Receptor IIIa (CD16a)
projectDescription: Fc γ-receptor IIIa (FcγRIIIa, or CD16a) is a receptor for the Fc region of IgG antibodies and plays an essential role in the regulation of antibody effector functions. While the activation of CD16a plays a role in a healthy immune response, dysregulated CD16a activity may contribute to tissue damage and chronic inflammation by over-activating immune cells or, conversely, by compromising the removal of immune complexes. Functionally distinct glycosylated forms of CD16a exist, with CD16a glycoforms modified with high mannose N-linked glycans at site N162 demonstrating a higher binding affinity for IgG compared to other forms of CD16a. Here, we developed and tested a nano-liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (nLC-MS/MS) parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) method for the site-specific study of CD16a glycosylation. The PRM method was tested by spiking recombinant CD16a (F158 or V158) into a complex matrix consisting of THP-1 cell lysate digest, then the CD16a glycopeptide PRM method was applied to measure statistically significant changes in site N162 N-glycan compositions corresponding to high affinity glycoforms of CD16a in a model of monocyte differentiation. Analyses were extended to the analysis of CD16a derived from human primary monocytes and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. CD16a site N162 N-glycosylation demonstrated remarkable similarity across the surveyed cell types, including in THP-1 cells – a monocyte cell line isolated from the peripheral blood of an acute monocytic leukemia patient, as well as primary human monocytes, and PBMCs. Critically, CD16a glycopeptide PRM facilitated measurement of changes in CD16a glycosylation at site N162, with high mannose N-glycan compositions, corresponding to high affinity glycoforms of CD16a, increasing in a model of monocyte differentiation into macrophages. Here, we have demonstrated the feasibility of utilizing a glycopeptide nLC-MS/MS-PRM targeted approach to study CD16a glycosylation in material from primary cells in a glycosylation site-specific manner. This strategy is well-suited for adaptation to clinical studies focused on understanding the role of CD16a glycosylation in physiology and disease, with a focus on immune disorders.
dataProcessingProtocol: Proteome Discoverer 2.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with an integrated Byonic v4.0.12 node (Protein Metrics Inc, Cupertino, CA, USA) were used for data analysis for glycopeptide identification from human FcγRIIIa and to stablish the precursors to target with the PRM method. For the analysis of FcγRIIIa enriched from THP-1 cells, monocytes and PBMCs only the F158 variant was analyzed, with data dependent strategy or targeted method. The reviewed human protein sequence database from UniProt (Homo sapiens Release 2023_03), with the inclusion of FcγRIIIa isoforms V158 and F158, and an N-glycan database consisting of 309 mammalian glycans were used for data searching. Parameters considered for the search include: 1 N-glycan per peptide (variable) and carbamidomethylation of cysteine (fixed), precursor tolerance: 10 ppm, fragment tolerance: 20 ppm, maximum number of missed cleavages: 6, cleaved residues: DEFLWY, common modifications max: 2, rare modification max: 1, false discovery rate (FDR): 1%. Following the Byonic analyses, glycopeptide assignments were filtered (Byonic score ≥200) and manually curated.  Skyline 29 (Skyline-daily version 24.1.1.202, University of Washington, USA) was used for quantification of selected glycopeptides from the PRM results. For identification of glycopeptides containing site N162, transitions from HexNAc (m/z 204.0867), HexNAc-H2O (m/z 186.0761), HexNAc-2H2O (m/z 168.0655), Hex-HexNAc (m/z 366.1395) ions, Y1 ion (peptide+HexNAc) and b/y-ions were used, while the Y1 ion (peptide+HexNAc) was used for quantification. On the other hand, due to their low relative abundance, for identification of glycopeptide harboring N45 transitions from HexNAc, HexNAc-H2O, HexNAc-2H2O, Hex-HexNAc ions, and at least one b- or y-ions were used, while the HexNAc ion was used for quantification. For glycopeptides harboring site N74, HexNAc, HexNAc-H2O, HexNAc-2H2O, Hex+HexNAc ions were used for identification and HexNAc ion for quantification. For Skyline analysis, the sequence of human CD16a (FcγRIIIa F158 or V158) from UniProt was utilized for the protein database. The peptide settings were as follows, enzyme specificity WFYLE, except when followed by P, for peptide modification: carbamidomethyl (C) and identified N-glycan compositions, a library was created from a survey search from Byonic (data dependent search), and target peptides manually edited including sequence and glycan compositions. The transition setting included: monoisotopic precursor mass and product ion mass, precursor charges were set as +3, +4 and +5, and ion charges were +1 and +2, ion type were y, b, and the precursor was also included. Y1 (peptide+ HexNAc) was included as a special ion. Ion match tolerance was 0.05 m/z. Subsequently, all transitions were manually inspected, and those that exceed +/-10 ppm error tolerance were discarded. Orbitrap was set as the analyzer for MS1 and MS2 filtering with resolving power 120,000 at 400 m/z for MS1 and 60,000 at 400 m/z for MS2. All assignments were manually curated considering peak shape of transitions from the same glycoform and retention time. The area under the curve (AUC) of the selected transition for quantification from each glycopeptide was exported from Skyline. Retention times were measured between runs to ensure consistency between replicates. Finally, AUCs from each glycopeptide containing a common asparagine residue were summed, and the summed area was used as the denominator to determine the relative abundance of each glycoform sharing the same N-glycosylation site.
sampleProcessingProtocol: An Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid mass spectrometer coupled with an EASY nLC 1200 system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) was used for both data dependent (DDA) and targeted nano-liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (nLC-MS/MS). Chromatographic separation was performed with  an Acclaim PepMap 100 (75 μm x 2 cm) trapping column and a PepMap RSLC C18 analytical column (2 μm, 100 Å, 75 μm × 15 cm)  with the following gradient: initial conditions 2% B, 2–6% B from 0 to 5 min, 6–35% B from 5 to 75 min, 35–60% B from 75 to 80 min, 60–95% B for 30 s, and 95% B for 9.5 min (solvents A and B consisted of 1% acetonitrile/99% water +0.1% formic acid and 80% acetonitrile/20% water + 0.1% formic acid, respectively). For all nLC-MS/MS experiments, four technical replicates (n=4) were performed unless otherwise noted. All MS1 spectra were acquired using a nano spray ionization source in positive mode applying 1900 V; transfer tube temperature: 275 ⁰C, RF lens 30%, and the Orbitrap was used as the mass analyzer with a resolution of 120,000 and quadrupole isolation set to ‘on’. The mass range was set to ‘normal’ (375-2000 m/z), and data was acquired in profile mode.  CD16a Titration Curves: Initially, 200 ng of THP-1 cell lysate digest spiked with different amounts of CD16a were analyzed via nano-liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry parallel reaction monitoring (nLC-MS/MS-PRM) method targeting a set of CD16a (FcγRIIIA V/F158) site Asn162 glycopeptide precursors from a list of previously described glycoforms16 to assess method performance. For the relative quantification of targeted glycoforms, a parallel reaction monitoring method was designed to acquire data alternatively in MS1 and MS2 modes targeting selected precursor within a retention time window (Supplementary Table 1) with the following parameters: MS1 settings were as described above with the following changes: AGC target set as standard; absolute AGC target 4x105, maximum injection time in ‘auto’ mode and 1 μscan. For MS2 scans, the isolation window for the quadrupole was 2 m/z, the activation type was HCD and 35% collision energy, orbitrap resolution: 50000, normal mass range, auto scan range mode, custom AGC target, 200 normalized AGC target (%), absolute AGC value of 1x105,100 ms for maximum injection time, 1 μscan, data type in profile mode and number of spectra (N) = 30. Defining Human Monocyte CD16a Glycopeptide Precursors: Given that the prior list of glycopeptide precursors was assembled from recombinant CD16a, we sought to determine if additional glycopeptides/glycoforms were present in THP-1-CD16+ cells, via an unbiased method. To achieve this, immunoaffinity-enriched CD16a from PMA-treated THP-1 cells with stable expression of human FcγRIIIa (THP1+CD16a cells) were analyzed via nLC-MS/MS using a data dependent method specifically designed to maximize the identification of glycopeptides, to sample CD16a glycoforms in an unbiased manner. The following parameters were set for glycopeptide discovery using a modified data dependent method to maximize the identification of glycopeptides. The MS1 settings were as described above with the following changes: custom AGC target; 200 for normalized AGC target (%), absolute AGC target 8 x 105, maximum injection time in ‘auto’ mode and 2 μscans. In MS2 scans, the isolation window for the quadrupole was 1.2 m/z units and the activation was HCD with a collision energy of 35%, AGC target set as standard and a maximum injection time of 35 ms, top speed of 3 sec, charge states 2-7, and dynamic exclusion ‘on’. The detection of ≥2 glycan oxonium ion peaks (m/z 138.0550, 144.0655, 168.0655, 186.0761, 204.0867, 274.0921, 292.1027, 366.1395, 512.1974; with 25 ppm mass tolerance) in the HCD spectrum triggered an EThcD MS2 scan and a sceHCD scan. EThcD was performed with the next settings: ETD with 20% supplemental activation, 30,000 resolution, mass range set as ‘high’, first scan set at 130 m/z, 1 μscan, custom AGC target, 200 normalized AGC target (%), maximum injection time set as ‘auto’ and data type in profile mode. Stepped collision energy HCD (sceHCD) was performed with 15, 30, and 40% collision energies, 15,000 resolution, 1 μscan, custom AGC target, 200 normalized AGC target (%), and 100 ms maximum injection time, and spectra were acquired in profile mode. PRM of CD16a Glycopeptides from Primary Human Monocytes and PBMCs: Following definition of CD16a glycoforms from primary cells, PRM analyses were conducted via a modified nano-liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry parallel reaction monitoring (nLC-MS/MS-PRM) method targeting CD16a sites N45, N74, and N162 glycopeptides with the same settings as above (see ‘CD16 Titration Curves’ section), with a modified set of precursors.

title: Characterizing the Effects of Protein Glycosylation Perturbation on Phosphorylation Signaling
projectDescription: This study investigates how engineered N-glycan remodeling affects phosphorylation signaling networks in human cells. We generated a glycoengineered HEK293 cell line (AI) with eliminated core fucosylation, enhanced sialylation, and reduced GlcNAc branching through sequential CRISPR/Cas9 knockouts (FUT8, MGAT4A/B, MGAT5, GMDS) and knock-in of sialuria-associated GNE mutations (R263L/R266Q), combined with stable overexpression of ST6Gal1, B4GalT1, MGAT1, and MGAT2. Both wildtype (WT) and AI cells were subjected to three treatment conditions in biological triplicate: normal growth in complete medium, 12-hour serum starvation, and 12-hour starvation followed by 30-minute serum re-stimulation (10% FBS). We performed integrated multi-omics profiling using TMT18-based quantitative proteomics to simultaneously characterize the global proteome (24 fractions), phosphoproteome (12 Fe-IMAC enriched fractions), and glycoproteome (12 MAX-enriched fractions) across all conditions. This dataset enables systematic interrogation of glycan-phosphorylation crosstalk and identifies glycan-dependent signaling rewiring in response to growth factor stimulation.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw data were searched using MS-PyCloud (global and phosphoproteomics), GPQuest (glycoproteomics), or Spectronaut (DIA data) against the UniProt human proteome with 10 ppm precursor and 20 ppm fragment mass tolerance, trypsin specificity (≤2 missed cleavages), peptide length 7-50 amino acids, and charge states +2 to +8. Fixed modifications: carbamidomethyl-Cys and TMT18 on N-termini/Lys. Variable modifications: Met oxidation (all datasets) plus Ser/Thr/Tyr phosphorylation (phosphoproteomics). PSMs were filtered to <1% FDR using target-decoy approach. Minimum requirements: 2 PSMs per peptide and 1 unique peptide per protein (global); 1 PSM per peptide and 1 unique peptide per protein (phospho/glyco). TMT reporter intensities were corrected using manufacturer-supplied factors. All downstream analyses were performed in R (v4.3.1). Data were log₂-transformed and normalized by robust median-centering. Missing values were imputed using DreamAI with KNN fallback. Quality control included intensity distribution checks, missing value diagnostics, and replicate correlation assessment (Spearman r > 0.85). Differential expression analysis used empirical Bayes linear modeling (limma package) with moderated t-statistics (pairwise) or F-statistics (multi-group). Significance thresholds: FDR < 0.05 (Benjamini-Hochberg) and |log₂FC| > 0.58. Cross-dataset integration retained top 500 features per dataset by F-statistic, requiring ≥70% completeness, then applied feature-wise z-score normalization. Functional enrichment employed over-representation analysis (ORA) with hypergeometric testing on KEGG and Reactome databases, analyzed separately for up/downregulated genes (adjusted p < 0.05). Kinase activity was inferred from PhosphoSitePlus and NetworKIN substrate annotations. Protein interaction networks were constructed via STRING (v11.5, confidence > 0.4) and clustered using MCODE (clusterMaker2 Cytoscape plugin: node score cutoff 0.1, degree cutoff 2, k-core 2). Visualizations generated using ggplot2, ComplexHeatmap, GraphPad Prism, and Cytoscape.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Cell pellets were lysed in 8M urea buffer containing protease inhibitors (aprotinin, leupeptin, PMSF), phosphatase inhibitors (NaF, PIC2/3), and PUGNAc through four freeze-thaw cycles. Protein concentrations were determined by BCA assay and 500 µg aliquots were reduced with 6 mM DTT (1h, 37°C), alkylated with 12 mM iodoacetamide (45 min, 25°C in dark), then digested with LysC (1:50, 2h, 25°C) followed by trypsin (1:50, overnight, 25°C) after 4-fold dilution. Digests were acidified to pH 3 with formic acid, desalted on C18 SepPak cartridges, and dried.For each TMT18 channel, 250 µg peptides in 100 µL of 100 mM HEPES pH 8.5 were labeled with 500 µg TMT18 reagent (1:2 ratio) for 1.5h at room temperature, quenched with 5% hydroxylamine (15 min), then pooled. Combined samples were desalted and fractionated by basic reversed-phase HPLC (bHPLC) on a Zorbax 300 Extend-C18 column using a 90-minute gradient (2-90% ACN in 5 mM ammonium formate, pH 10), yielding 96 fractions concatenated into 24 fractions. A 5% aliquot of each fraction was reserved for global proteomics; the remaining 95% was further concatenated into 12 fractions for sequential enrichments.Phosphopeptides were enriched by Fe³⁺-IMAC using Ni-NTA-derived beads in 80% ACN/0.1% TFA, washed, and eluted with 500 mM K₂HPO₄ (pH 7.0) onto C18 Stage Tips, then eluted with 50% ACN/0.1% FA. IMAC flow-through was acidified, desalted on C18 SepPak, eluted with 50% and 95% ACN/0.1% TFA, adjusted to 95% ACN/1% TFA, and loaded onto Oasis MAX cartridges for glycopeptide enrichment. After washing with 95% ACN/1% TFA, intact glycopeptides were eluted with 50% ACN/0.1% TFA. All fractions were dried and reconstituted in 3% ACN/0.1% FA before LC-MS/MS analysis.

title: Thermal Proteome Prodiling and Glycoproteomics of U937 cells
projectDescription: Protein glycosylation regulates essential cellular processes including protein folding, stability, and cell-cell interactions; however, how aberrant glycosylation impacts protein function and interaction networks remains poorly understood. Here we combine mass spectrometry-based proteomics, chemical glycobiology, and molecular dynamics simulations to systematically investigate glycosylation dependent protein stability and function. By perturbing the secretory pathway at defined steps, we generated proteins with distinct glycan structures and analyzed their functional consequences using thermal proteome profiling (TPP). This approach revealed that cells mount convergent stress responses to diverse glycosylation perturbations, characterized by coordinated trafficking reorganization. This reorganization effectively redirects protein flux from secretion toward degradation. We further identified that perturbing terminal glycan modifications, particularly sialylation and fucosylation, exerts the most profound effects on cell surface protein function. We studied in detail how loss of fucosylation restricts the conformational dynamics of key domains in integrin alpha 4, reducing VCAM-1 binding affinity and suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy for multiple sclerosis. Overall, our systematic approach uncovered extensive complexity in how glycosylation regulates protein function beyond simple glycoform identification and provides a resource for dissecting essential glycan-protein relationships.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw LC-MS/MS data were processed using two complementary search strategies to maximize peptide and glycopeptide identification. For glycopeptide analysis, pGlyco3 (v3.1)54 was employed using its N-glycosylation HCD fragmentation workflow with the default human N-glycan database (pGlyco-N-Human.gdb). For global proteomics and TMT quantification, FragPipe (v20.0) was used, applying the standard TMT10-MS2 workflow55 of MSFragger (v3.8)56 for database searching, IonQuant (v1.9.8) for quantification, and Philosopher (v5.0.0) for statistical validation. Prior to FragPipe analysis, raw files were converted to mzML format using MSConvert (ProteoWizard)57. Both search engines queried the UniProt human reference proteome (UP000005640, downloaded 2023-10-02) supplemented with common contaminant sequences and reversed decoy sequences for false discovery rate (FDR) estimation. Search parameters included: trypsin digestion with up to two missed cleavages; peptide length between 7-50 (MSFragger) or 7-40 (pGlyco3) amino acids; precursor mass tolerance of 10 ppm; fragment ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm. Fixed modifications included carbamidomethylation of cysteine (+57.021 Da) and TMT10plex labeling of lysine residues and peptide N-termini (+229.163 Da). Variable modifications included oxidation of methionine (+15.995 Da) and protein N-terminal acetylation (+42.011 Da). For MSFragger and pGlyco3 results, peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) were filtered to 1% FDR using target-decoy competition.
sampleProcessingProtocol: TPP Peptide fractions were reconstituted in loading buffer (0.2% formic acid in MS-grade water) and analyzed using an UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The chromatography system was configured with a trapping cartridge (Acclaim PepMap 100 C18, 5 μm, 100 Å, 300 μm × 20 mm; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and an analytical column (Aurora Series AUR3-25075C18-TS, 25 cm × 75 μm i.d., 1.7 μm C18; IonOptics). Peptides were loaded onto the trapping cartridge at 5 μL/min with solvent A (0.2% formic acid in water) for 5 min, then separated on the analytical column at 300 nL/min using a 95-min gradient. The gradient profile was as follows: 2% solvent B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile) for 4 min; 2-4% B over 2 min; 4-28% B over 60.5 min; 28-40% B over 6.5 min; 40-95% B over 5 min; maintained at 95% B for 5 min; followed by re-equilibration at 2% B for 12 min. Peptides were ionized using an EASY-Spray ion source operated at 1.85 kV with the column temperature maintained at 45°C and the inlet capillary at 325°C. Data-dependent acquisition (DDA) was performed with the following parameters: MS1 survey scans were acquired from 400-1,450 m/z at 120,000 resolution (at m/z 200) with an automatic gain control (AGC) target of 4 × 10⁵, maximum injection time of 50 ms, and RF lens setting of 60%. The top 10 most intense precursors with charge states between 2+ and 8+ were selected for MS2 fragmentation using a 1.0 m/z isolation window. MS2 scans were acquired in the Orbitrap at 50,000 resolution with an AGC target of 1 × 10⁵, maximum injection time of 120 ms, and normalized HCD collision energy of 38%. The first mass was set to 120 m/z to ensure TMT reporter ion detection. Monoisotopic precursor selection was enabled, and dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s with a ±10 ppm mass tolerance window. N-Glyco-proteomics Glycopeptide fractions were reconstituted in loading buffer (0.2% formic acid in MS-grade water) and analyzed using an UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The chromatography system was configured with a trapping cartridge (Acclaim PepMap 100 C18, 5 μm, 100 Å, 300 μm × 20 mm; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and an analytical column (Aurora Series AUR3-25075C18-TS, 25 cm × 75 μm i.d., 1.7 μm C18; IonOptics). Glycopeptides were loaded onto the trapping cartridge at 5 μL/min with solvent A (0.1% formic acid in water) for 5 min, then separated on the analytical column at 300 nL/min using a 120-min gradient optimized for glycopeptide separation. The gradient profile was as follows: 1% solvent B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile) for 6.5 min; 5-28% B over 90 min; 28-95% B over 4.5 min; maintained at 95% B for 4 min; followed by re-equilibration at 1% B for 15 min. Peptides were ionized using an EASY-Spray ion source operated at 1.85 kV with the column temperature maintained at 45°C and the inlet capillary at 325°C. Data-dependent acquisition (DDA) was performed with the following parameters: MS1 survey scans were acquired from 500-1,800 m/z at 120,000 resolution (at m/z 200) with an automatic gain control (AGC) target of 4 × 10⁵, maximum injection time of 80 ms, and RF lens setting of 60%. The top 10 most intense precursors with charge states between 2+ and 8+ were selected for MS2 fragmentation using a 2.0 m/z isolation window to accommodate glycopeptide isotopic distributions. MS2 scans were acquired in the Orbitrap at 60,000 resolution with an AGC target of 1 × 10⁵, maximum injection time of 200 ms, and normalized HCD collision energy of 35%. The scan range was set to 120-4,000 m/z to capture both peptide fragments and glycan oxonium ions. Monoisotopic precursor selection was enabled, and dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s with a ±10 ppm mass tolerance window.

title: Dose-Dependent Inhibition of Protein Glycosylation Reveals Crosstalk Between Glycosylation and Phosphorylation in EGF Signaling Pathways
projectDescription: Protein glycosylation and phosphorylation play critical roles in regulating diverse cellular processes, yet their interplay remains underexplored. This study employed a dose-dependent glycosylation inhibition to investigate the function of glycosylation, especially in phosphorylation in epidermal growth factor (EGF) signaling. Using quantitative proteomics, we analyzed global protein expression, glycopeptides, and phosphopeptides in EGF-stimulated and unstimulated conditions. Results revealed that glycosylation inhibition disrupted phosphorylation patterns in EGF-regulated pathways. Notably, 215 EGF-regulated phosphopeptides exhibited dose-dependent changes, with pathways such as ERBB, MAPK, and mTOR signaling being significantly affected. Protein-protein interaction analysis highlighted glycosylation-dependent modulation of phosphorylation in cytoskeletal remodeling and growth factor signaling. Correlation analysis identified site-specific glycopeptides, such as Asn568 of EGFR, that influenced phosphorylation of downstream signaling proteins. Additionally, individual proteins like RCN1 and SLC4A7 demonstrated glycosylation and phosphorylation regulated patterns. These findings underscored the role of glycosylation in maintaining phosphorylation-dependent signaling fidelity, providing insights into function of glycosylation on cell signaling pathways.
dataProcessingProtocol: LC-MS/MS analysis All LC-MS/MS data were acquired using an EvoSep system coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Ascend mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) operating in data-dependent acquisition (DDA) mode. TMT-labeled global proteome, phosphoproteome, and glycoproteome fractions were loaded onto Evotips and separated on a PepSep C18 column (15 cm × 150 µm, 1.5 µm) at 50 °C using a 30 SPD gradient.  For global and phosphoproteomic samples, MS1 scans were collected at 60,000 resolution across 350–1800 m/z with an AGC target of 4×10⁵, max injection time of 50 ms, RF lens of 30%, and charge states 2–6. Dynamic exclusion was set at 45 s. A 2-s cycle time was used, selecting the most abundant precursors for MS2. MS2 spectra were acquired at 50,000 resolution using HCD at 34% collision energy, 0.7 m/z isolation width, AGC 2×10⁵, and max injection time of 100 ms.  For glycoproteomic samples, MS1 scans were acquired at 60,000 resolution from 500–2000 m/z with AGC 5×10⁵. MS2 scans used 50,000 resolution, HCD 35%, 0.7 m/z isolation width, AGC 1×10⁵, and 100 ms injection time. Source settings were 1.8 kV spray voltage and 300 °C ion transfer tube temperature. Additional glycoproteomic runs employed stepped HCD energies (25/35/45%), MS1 at 120,000 resolution, and MS2 at 30,000 resolution (AGC 3×10⁵, 64 ms injection time). Charge states 2–8 and a dynamic exclusion of 45 s (±10 ppm) were applied.  MaxQuant analysis for global, phospho-, and glycoproteomic data Raw files were processed with MaxQuant (v2.4.14.0) using the UniProtKB human reference proteome (downloaded 2024-02-29). Trypsin specificity was used with up to 3 missed cleavages for global samples and 4 for PTM datasets. Fixed modification: carbamidomethyl-Cys; variable modifications: Met oxidation and N-terminal acetylation. Phospho-Ser/Thr/Tyr was allowed for phosphoproteomic datasets. Peptides required ≥6 amino acids, with up to 5 modifications per peptide. Modified peptides required an Andromeda score ≥40 and delta score ≥6.  A 1% PSM FDR was applied using a target–decoy strategy. For PTM datasets, the protein-level FDR was set to 100% to maintain a 1% FDR at the peptide level; protein groups were not used for PTM quantification. For global proteomics, the protein FDR was set at 1%. TMT isotope impurities were corrected automatically. The phosphoproteome evidence file and global proteome proteinGroups file were used for quantification.  Glycoproteomic data processing (GPQuest)  DDA glycoproteomic raw files were converted to mzML using ProteoWizard (peak picking enabled). Glycopeptide identification was performed using GPQuest 3.0 with a human N-glycan library and the same UniProtKB database.  Search parameters included: precursor tolerance 10 ppm, fragment tolerance 20 ppm, trypsin digestion with up to 2 missed cleavages, peptide length 7–50 aa, and precursor charge states +2 to +8. b- and y-ions were considered for peptide fragmentation, requiring at least 6 matched peaks. Carbamidomethyl-Cys was set as fixed and Met oxidation as variable. Identifications were filtered at 1% PSM FDR.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Cell culture and treatments A498 cells (ATCC HTB-44) were cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO₂ in MEM (Gibco 11095080) containing 10% FBS and 1% Pen/Strep. For tunicamycin treatment, cells were exposed to 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, and 10 μM tunicamycin (Selleck S7894), plus a DMSO control, for 24 h. Afterward, cells were treated with or without 50 ng/ml EGF (Sigma E9644) for 15 min. Cells were washed with cold PBS and harvested, yielding approximately 4 million cells per condition.  Protein extraction and digestion Cell pellets were lysed on ice using 100 μl of buffer containing 8 M urea, 75 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 1 mM EDTA, protease inhibitors (2 μg/ml aprotinin, 10 μg/ml leupeptin, 1 mM PMSF), phosphatase inhibitors (10 mM NaF, PIC2 and PIC3 at 1:100), and 20 μM PUGNAc. Lysis included vortexing and repeated incubation cycles at 4 °C. Lysates were cleared by centrifugation (20,000 g, 10 min) and protein levels were measured by BCA assay. Proteins were adjusted to 5 μg/μl, and 500 μg aliquots were prepared.  Proteins were reduced with 6 mM DTT (1 h, 37 °C) and alkylated with 12 mM IAA (45 min, dark). Samples were diluted 1:4 with 50 mM Tris pH 8.0 to reduce urea below 2 M. Proteins were digested with LysC (1:50, 2 h, 25 °C), followed by trypsin (1:50, ~14 h, 25 °C). Digestion was stopped by adding formic acid to 1% final concentration (pH 3). Samples were diluted to 1 ml with 0.1% FA, centrifuged to remove precipitates, desalted by C18 SPE, and dried.  TMT labeling For each TMT18 channel, 250 μg peptides (measured by peptide BCA) were dissolved in 100 μl 100 mM HEPES pH 8.5. TMT reagent was reconstituted in anhydrous ACN, and 500 μg reagent was added per sample (1:2 peptide:TMT). Labeling occurred for 1.5 h at room temperature with shaking. Reactions were quenched with 5% hydroxylamine (15 min). Labeled samples were pooled, dried, reconstituted in 3% ACN/0.1% FA, pH-adjusted to 3 if needed, and cleaned again on SepPak cartridges.  Peptide fractionation Dried peptides were resuspended in 20 mM ammonium formate (pH 10) with 2% ACN and separated by basic reversed-phase HPLC (Agilent 1200) on a Zorbax Extend-C18 column. Peptides were eluted using a multi-step gradient of Solvent A (2% ACN, 5 mM ammonium formate) and Solvent B (90% ACN, 5 mM ammonium formate). Fractions were collected and concatenated into 24 pools. Five percent of each fraction was dried and resuspended in 3% ACN/0.1% FA for global proteomics; the remaining material was used for phosphopeptide enrichment.  Phosphopeptide enrichment (Fe-IMAC) Concatenated peptides were resuspended in 80% ACN/0.1% TFA and incubated with Fe³⁺-NTA IMAC beads for 30 min. After removing unbound peptides, beads were washed and transferred to C18 StageTips. Phosphopeptides were eluted with 500 mM potassium phosphate (pH 7.0), cleaned on C18 StageTips, dried, and reconstituted in 3% ACN/0.1% FA for LC-MS/MS.  Glycopeptide enrichment (ZIC-HILIC) ZIC-HILIC micro-columns were prepared in-house and equilibrated with 80% ACN/1% TFA. Peptides were loaded, washed with the same buffer, and glycopeptides were eluted using 0.1% TFA. Eluates were dried and stored at –80 °C before LC-MS/MS analysis.

title: N-glycosylation of AXL receptor tyrosine kinase regulates its stability, phosphorylation and oncogenic function
projectDescription: AXL, a receptor tyrosine kinase implicated in tumor progression, undergoes post-translational modifications that regulate its activity and stability. In this study, we have analyzed AXL immunoprecipitated from cell lines by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)-based glycoproteomics and show that AXL is extensively N-glycosylated in breast and ovarian cancer cells, existing predominantly as two isoforms corresponding to high-mannose and complex-type glycans. The extracellular cleaved soluble form of AXL (sAXL) primarily carries complex N-glycans. LC-MS/MS–based glycoproteomics analysis identified five glycosylation sites (Asn43, Asn157, Asn198, Asn339, and Asn345) with extensive microheterogeneity, including sialylation, fucosylation, and bisecting GlcNAc modifications. Overall, our results demonstrate that N-glycosylation is essential for AXL stability, localization, and oncogenic signaling, offering new insights into how glycosylation regulates receptor tyrosine kinases function in cancer.
dataProcessingProtocol: Database searching for N-glycopeptides was performed using publicly available software pGlyco Version 3. Human N-glycan databases already available with the software were used, and UniProt Human Reviewed protein sequences (20,432 entries, downloaded February 1, 2021) were used as protein sequence FASTA file. Respective enzyme-specificity was set for searching with 2 missed cleavages allowed, and precursor and fragment tolerance were set to 10 and 20 ppm, respectively. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was set as fixed modification and deamidation of asparagine and glutamine were set as variable modifications. The results were filtered to retain entries that had <1% FDR at glycopeptide level. MS/MS spectra were manually verified for several glycan oxonium ions and quality. All sialic acid-containing glycopeptide spectra were verified for presence of sialic acid–specific oxonium ions at m/z 274.09, 292.10 and/or 657.23. Data were simultaneously searched using Sequest in Proteome Discoverer 3.0 to identify non-glycosylated peptides.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Immunoprecipitation of AXL and proteomics sample preparation: Cell lysates (1 mg protein per sample) from MDA-MB-231 and HEK293T-AXL-HA cells were subjected to immunoprecipitation. AXL–HA was pulled down using anti-HA agarose beads, while endogenous AXL was immunoprecipitated with anti-AXL antibody (#AF154, R&D) and protein G agarose (Invitrogen; #15920-010). Enriched AXL was reduced with DTT and alkylated with IAA, and then digested using sequencing-grade trypsin (Promega; V5111), chymotrypsin (Promega; V1061), GluC (NEB; P8100S), or trypsin–chymotrypsin combinations. Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS): Peptides generated from on-beads digestion of immunoprecipitated AXL samples were analyzed by LC-MS/MS on an Orbitrap Eclipse, Ascend or Exploris 480 instrument. Briefly, peptides were separated by liquid chromatography on an EASY-Spray column (75 μm × 50 cm, PepMap RSLC C18, Thermo Fisher Scientific) packed with 2 μm C18 particles, maintained at 50°C. We used 0.1% formic acid in water (solvent A) and 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile (solvent B) as solvents. Peptides were trapped on a trap column (100 mm × 2 cm, Acclaim PepMap100 Nano-Trap, Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a flow rate of 20 μL/min. LC separation was performed at a flow rate of 300 nL/min, and the following gradient was used: equilibration at 3% solvent B from 0 to 4 minutes, 3% to 10% sol B from 4 to 10 minutes, 10% to 35% sol B from 10.1 to 125 minutes, 35% to 80% sol B from 125 to 145 minutes, followed by equilibration for next run at 5% sol B for 5 minutes. Experiments were done in data-dependent acquisition mode with top 15 ions isolated at a window of m/z 0.7 and default charge state of +2. Precursors with charge states ranging from +2 to +7 were considered for MS/MS events. Normalized stepped collision energy was applied to fragment precursors at energies of 15%, 25%, and 40%. Precursor ions were acquired in the Orbitrap mass analyzer in m/z range of 350–2,000 for glycoproteomics and m/z 350–1,800 for proteomics at a resolution of 120,000 (at m/z 200). Automatic gain control (AGC) for MS and MS/MS were 106 and 1 × 105, and injection times to reach AGC were 50 ms and 250 ms, respectively. Exclude isotopes feature was set to “on,” and 60-second dynamic exclusion was applied. Data acquisition was performed with option of “lock mass” (m/z 441.12002) for all data.

title: LC-MS/MS of glycopeptides with oligo-mannose glycans
projectDescription: We report the development of an enzymatic pipeline that generates glycopeptides carrying homogeneous eukaryotic N-glycans (oligomannose and complex) that are not accessible by alternative methodologies.
dataProcessingProtocol: The mass spectrometer was operated under data‐dependent acquisition (DDA), one scan cycle comprised of a full scan MS survey spectrum, followed by up to 12 sequential HCD MS/MS on the most intense signals above a threshold of 1e4. Full‐scan MS spectra (600–2000 m/z) were acquired in the FT‐Orbitrap at a resolution of 70,000 at 400 m/z, while HCD MS/MS spectra were recorded in the FT‐Orbitrap at a resolution of 35,000 at 400 m/z. HCD was performed with a target value of 1e5 and normalization collision energy 32 was applied. AGC target values were 5e5 for full FTMS. For all experiments, dynamic exclusion was used with a single repeat count, 15 s repeat duration, and 30 s exclusion duration. The XIC and MS profile were shown by Xcalibur. All raw data were searched against a database containing user-provided sequences via Byonic 5.10 (Protein Metrics) search engine with the consideration of amidation at the C-terminal and the corresponding modification at the N-terminal of either 5-CF or TAMRA. The mass error for MS1 was 10 ppm and 0.02 Daltons for MS2.
sampleProcessingProtocol: We confirm correct assembly of enzymatically generated phytyl-pyrophosphate-linked oligosaccharides by transferring the latter onto fluorescently labelled acceptor sequon. We achieve this using purified yeast oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex or the single-subunit OSTs A or B from Trypanosoma brucei. For yeast OST-catalyzed reaction, we employed the peptide TAMRA-YANATS-NH2, while for TbSTT3A-catalyzed reactions, 5-carboxyfluorescein-GSDANYTYTQ-NH2 was used. Generally, peptide glycosylation was carried out at 30ºC with 5-10 µM fluorescent peptide and 100-200 nM OST enzyme. The reactions were performed in buffer containing 150 mM NaCl, 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 10 mM MnCl2, 0.035% DDM, and 0.007% CHS. Glycopeptides were analyzed by LC-MS/MS to assess correct composition. LC-MS/MS analysis  (n=1 per glycopeptide) was done at the Functional Genomics Center Zurich. Samples were diluted 10-fold with 0.1% formic acid in H2O and 2 uL of samples were analyzed on a calibrated FUSION mass spectrometer (Thermo Fischer Scientific) coupled to a nano‐Acquity UPLC system (Waters). Glycopeptides were resuspended in 2.5% acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid and loaded onto a nanoEase M/Z Symmetry C18, Trap Column (180 μm x 20 mm, 100 Å, 5 μm particle size) and separated on a nanoEase M/Z HSS C18 T3 (75 μm × 150 mm, 100 Å, 1.8 μm particle size), at a constant flow rate of 300 nL min‐1, with a column temperature of 50 °C and a linear gradient of 2−35% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid in 20 min, and then 35‐98% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid in 5 min, and then held isocratically for another 5 min.

title: Theileria parva Muguga (TpM) schizonts LC-MS/MS
projectDescription: The apicomplexan parasite Theileria parva (Tp) causes East Coast Fever (ECF), an often fatal tick-borne disease especially for Bos taurus cattle breeds that causes substantial economic losses for cattle farmers in sub-Saharan Africa. Replacement of the currently employed live vaccine with a more standardised, stable, affordable, and cross-protective subunit vaccine has not yet been successful and requires the identification of additional suitable parasite antigens. Carbohydrate-based molecules play an important role in the survival and establishment of pathogens including protozoan parasites and can represent strong virulence factors. The current knowledge of the glycobiology of Tp, however, is very limited which led us to investigate the glycosylation potential of Tp in this study. Screening of isolated Tp Muguga (TpM) schizonts with C-type lectin (-like) receptors identified recognition of the parasites by ruminant but not murine Macrophage C-type lectin (MCL). This suggested the presence of carbohydrate-associated schizont surface molecules. Specific binding of isolated schizonts by WGA but not ConA further suggested the presence of terminal GlcNAc residues on the surface of the parasites which is in alignment with the identification of a minimal N-glycosylation machinery in TpM schizonts. LC-MS/MS analyses of either HILIC-HPLC or WGA enriched peptides from parasite protein fractions identified eight predicted N-glycopeptides and two predicted O-glycopeptides. While putative parasite O-glycans were assigned with high confidence, assignments of putative N-glycans to parasite proteins were less confident. Confirmation of both the assignment and the composition of predicted parasite glycans requires further analyses.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw data of C18-purified AP and DP samples were searched against proteomes of T. parva (Taxon ID: 5875; 2790 entries) and B. taurus (Taxon ID: 9913; 37504 entries) using Proteome Discoverer (version 2.4.1.15; Thermo Fisher Scientific). Furthermore, all LC-ESI-MS/MS data were also analysed using the FragPipe Software version 220 with the MSFragger search engine (Nesvilab) for glycopeptide identification. Prediction of signal peptides and transmembrane domains as well as N-glycosylation sites for identified proteins was performed with the SignalP-6.0, Deep TMHMM-1.0 algorithms and NetNGlyc - 1.0, respectively, developed by DTU Health Tech.
sampleProcessingProtocol: To determine potential parasite glycans, proteins from AP and DP fractions of TpM schizonts were subjected to glycoproteomic analyses using mass spectrometry (MS). Briefly, protein samples were denatured in reducing buffer (8 M urea, 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, 5 mM DTT, pH 7.8) and treated with trypsin (Promega) overnight at 37°C. The resulting peptides were purified using hand-packed C18 cartridges (50% acetonitrile with 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid as eluent) and evaporated to dryness using a speed-vac concentrator. Dried peptides were resuspended in HPLC-grade water and analysed on an Autoflex Speed MALDI-TOF MS (Bruker Daltonics) using α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid or 6-aza-2-thiothymine as matrix. The instrument was calibrated with the Bruker Peptide Calibration Standard II.   Additionally, AP and DP samples were analysed by nanoLC-ESI-MS(/MS), using a Q Exactive HF Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to a nano-HPLC Ultimate 3000 RSLC system (Dionex) for peptide separation. MS full scans were performed in the ultrahigh-field Orbitrap mass analyser in ranges m/z 350−2,000 with a resolution of 60,000, the maximum injection time (MIT) was 50 ms and the automatic gain control (AGC) was set to 3e^6. The top ten intense ions of each MS scan were selected for gas-phase fragmentation using high energy collision dissociation (HCD). For each MS/MS scan, the AGC was set at 5e^4 and the MIT was 50 ms. Dynamic exclusion of precursor ion masses over a time window of 30s was used to reduce MS/MS data redundancy.  Overall glycopeptide populations of AP and DP samples were enriched using hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC), as described recently. In brief, dried (glyco)peptides were re-suspended in 50 µL of 80% acetonitrile containing 1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and fractionated using a TSK-Amide 80 column (4.6 x 250 mm, 5 µm, Tosoh). A linear gradient was developed from 80% acetonitrile with 0.1% TFA to 50% acetonitrile with 0.1% TFA over 30 minutes, at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. Fractions of 1 mL were collected using a fraction collector (Shimadzu). Late-eluting HILIC fractions (minutes 20–39) were pooled and lyophilised prior to LC-MS/MS analysis.  Enriched (glyco)peptides were resuspended in 20 µL of 0.1% formic acid and separated by reversed-phase nano-LC using a nanoEase M/Z HSS T3 column (100 Å, 1.8 µm, 300 µm × 150 mm; Waters). MS/MS analysis was performed on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a standard H-ESI source, operated in positive ion mode. MS spectra were acquired in the m/z range of 350–1500 at a resolution of 60,000. Data-dependent MS/MS acquisition was triggered for precursor ions with charge states 2–6 and intensities above 800,000, using an isolation window of 1.4 m/z (offset 0.5 m/z), with a normalised AGC target of 200%. Fragmentation was performed using stepped HCD. MS/MS scans were acquired at a resolution of 30,000 with the first fixed mass set at m/z 120.

title: A comprehensive landscape of human organ N-glycoproteome
projectDescription: N-glycosylation, as a common post-translational modification with enormous structures, plays key roles in protein folding, cellular recognition and signaling pathways. State-of-the-art mass spectrometry-based N-glycoproteomics has enabled deep N-glycoproteome characterization of various human organs. However, a comprehensive N-glycoproteome landscape of human organs remains lacking. Here we present a systematic human N-glycoproteome atlas spanning 18 organs/tissues with identification of 31,003 intact N-glycopeptides, corresponding to 14,043 N-glycan monosaccharide compositions on 5,539 N-glycosites of 3,681 N-glycoproteins. Tissue-specific glycosylation patterns, novel glycoforms and crosstalk between sialylation and fucosylation are observed. This atlas, complemented by a unified multi-software analysis framework, provides insights into organ-specific glycobiology and establishes a fundamental reference for understanding physiological glycosylation characteristics of human tissues.
dataProcessingProtocol: A comprehensive glycoproteomic analysis was performed utilizing a custom-built glycan database comprising 6,709 structures derived from 603 distinct compositions in gPeptide format. MS raw data from three technical replicates per sample were searched against the UniProt Homo sapiens reference proteome (version 2023-07-28, containing 20,423 protein sequences) and glycan database. Searches were performed using trypsin as the proteolytic enzyme, allowing up to two missed cleavages. Mass tolerance was set to 20 ppm for both precursor and fragment ions. Other parameters included isotopic peak abundance cutoff (IPACO)≥40%, isotopic peak abundance deviation (IPAD)≥50%, percentage of matched peptide backbone product ions (p-PMPs)≥10%, matched peptide backbone product ions (MPs)≥6, isotopic peaks (IPs coverage) ≥10%, abundance coverage≥16%, matched fragment ions of the N-glycan moiety≥1, TopN hits N = 2 (Top1 hits have the lowest p score), Y1 ions Top4. Spectrum-level false discovery rate (FDR) was controlled at 1% using the target-decoy approach. The quantitative extracted ion chromatogram (EIC) of each ID was extracted by Skyline.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The samples were thawed on ice. After cutting the tissue into pieces while keeping it on ice, lysis buffer (0.1 M Tris/HCl, 4% SDS, pH 8.0) and protease inhibitor (1% v/v) were added. The sample was then homogenized for 1 minute at 8,000 g and incubated on ice for 30 minutes to obtain lysates. Lysates were centrifuged at 14, 000 g for 30 min at 4 °C and the supernatant was then mixed with cold acetone (1:5, v/v) at -20 °C for 3 h in order to obtain protein precipitation. After redissolving with 8M urea, protein concentrations were determined by BCA assay. Proteins (1 mg/ml) were reduced in 10 mM DTT for 20 min at 55 °C, alkylated in 20 mM IAA for 30 min at RT in the dark; DTT was then added to a final concentration of 10 mM to terminate the reaction. Samples were diluted with 50 mM ABC and digested with trypsin at a 1:50 enzyme-to-substrate ratio overnight at 37 °C. Tryptic peptides were desalted by C18 (Phenomenex Jupiter, 15 μm, 300 Å) solid phase extraction (SPE) columns and dried in a SpeedVac (Thermo Scientific). The ZIC-HILIC (Merck, 5 μm, 200 Å) SPE column was equilibrated three times with 300 uL of 80% ACN, 1% TFA (v/v). Tryptic peptides were redissolved in 300 uL 80% ACN, 0.1% TFA (v/v) and loaded on the ZIC-HILIC column for five times; after wash with 80%ACN, 0.1% TFA (v/v), intact glycopeptides were eluted in 300 uL 0.1% TFA and 200 uL 50 mM ABC. The eluants were combined and dried in the SpeedVac.

title: IgM hyposialylation drives podocyte injury in pediatric and young adult patients with podocytopathies
projectDescription: Altered immunoglobulin glycosylation has been implicated in antibody-mediated podocytopathies, yet the functional impact of IgM sialylation remains unclear. Previous evidence suggested that circulating cationic or hyposialylated IgM may contribute to podocyte injury in idiopathic nephrotic syndrome (iNS). Serum IgM from pediatric and young adult patients with podocytopathies, membranous nephropathy (MN), lupus nephritis (LN), and healthy controls were analyzed by lectin-based ELISA using a panel of six biotinylated lectins to detect terminal N-glycan residues. Among these, Sambucus nigra agglutinin (SNA) binds α2,6-linked sialic acid, and Ricinus communis agglutinin I (RCA-I) recognizes β1,4-linked galactose. Serum levels of the α2,6-sialyltransferase ST6GAL1 and the sialidases neuraminidase-1 (NEU1) and neuraminidase-3 (NEU3) were quantified. Cultured human podocytes were exposed to patient-derived, control, or enzymatically modified IgM (desialylated/resialylated) and analyzed by confocal microscopy, quantitative proteomics, phosphoproteomics, and metabolic assays. IgM from patients with podocytopathies showed reduced SNA binding, which inversely correlated with proteinuria (r = −0.69, P < 0.0001) and with serum sialidases NEU1/NEU3 (r = −0.67/−0.59, P < 0.0001). In paired samples, SNA reactivity decreased during relapse and normalized in remission, indicating dynamic modulation with disease activity. ST6GAL1 was undetectable in all groups. In contrast, PLA2R1-positive MN, in which pathogenic antibodies target podocyte PLA2R1, displayed reduced RCA-I binding. Podocytes exposed to hyposialylated or desialylated IgM exhibited actin disorganization, loss of nephrin signal, increased lipid peroxidation, and decreased ATP synthesis. In contrast, resialylated IgM preserved morphology and metabolism comparable to controls. Proteomic and phosphoproteomic profiling revealed enrichment of MAPK, mTOR, AMPK, and cytoskeletal remodeling pathways. IgM hyposialylation, driven by extracellular sialidases up-regulation, correlates with disease activity and promotes oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cytoskeletal remodeling in podocytes, identifying immune glycan remodeling as a modifiable determinant of podocyte injury and a potential biomarker of disease activity.
dataProcessingProtocol: All DIA raw files were processed with Spectronaut version 18 using a library-free approach (directDIA) under default settings. The library was generated against the Uniprot Human database (release UP000005640_9606 June 2024, 104602 Entries). Carbamidomethylation was selected as a fixed modification, while methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation were selected as variable modifications. False discovery rate (FDR) of peptide-spectrum match (PSM) and peptide/protein groups were set to 0.01. For quantification, Precursor Filtering was set to Identified (Qvalue) and MS2 was chosen as quantity MS-level.  After log2 conversion, a normal distribution was used to impute missing values, and the entire dataset was normalized using the quantile method. The normalized dataset was analyzed using unsupervised hierarchical clustering, including principal component analysis and k-means clustering, to identify outliers and dissimilarities among samples. ANOVA test for unpaired samples was used to identify statistically significant proteins between podocyte cells treated with iNS IgM-derived (iNS), CTR IgM-derived, without modification (CTR) or desialylated (Desialylated). Then, to identify the proteins that maximized discrimination between iNS and CTR, or Desialylated and CTR, or Desialylated and iNS, we used t-test analysis. For both analyses, proteins were considered statistically significantly expressed for power values of 80% and adjusted p-values ≤ 0.05 after correction for multiple interactions (Benjamini-Hochberg method). Volcano plots were used to visualize the results of the t-test analysis, with the threshold line determined by the function y = |c/(x − x0)|. Gene ontology analysis was performed to identify the enriched pathways through the active subnetworks using the PathFindR package. Kinase enrichment analysis (KEA) was also performed using the statistically significant proteins as substrates to predict kinases potentially involved in regulating the phosphorylation signal in each comparison. The Coral App was used to visualize the kinome tree of proteome profile. For the lectin ELISA, lipid peroxidation, and ATP synthesis differences across all clinical groups were determined using the Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's correction. Pearson’s correlation coefficients were calculated to assess the relationships between UPCR, SNA reactivity, and serum NEU1 and NEU3 levels. Paired samples collected at <0.2 and >3.5 gr/day proteinuria were compared using the Wilcoxon test. For the kinome assay, differences across all conditions were determined using a t-test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. All statistical tests were performed using OriginLab Pro version 2022b and R version 4.3.3 software.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Podocyte cells were lysed, reduced and alkylated in 50 ul LYSE buffer (Preomics) at 95°C for 10 min and sonicated with an Ultrasonic Processor  UP200St (Hielscher), 3 cycles of 30 sec.  Proteins were isolated and digested by PAC method automated on a KingFisher™ Apex robot (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in 96-well format as described in [ref ]. Briefly, the tip plate was stored in plate #1. Lysate samples were stored in plate #2, in a final concentration of 70% acetonitrile and with magnetic beads in a protein/bead ratio of 1:4 (1:1 SpeedBead Magnetic Carboxylate, 45152105050250 and 65152105050250). Washing solutions were in plates #3–5 (acetonitrile), plate #6 (70% Ethanol) and plate #7 (isopropanol). Plate #8 contained 100 ul digestion solution of 25 mM Tris HCl pH 8, LysC (Wako) in an enzyme/protein ratio of 1:100 (w/w) and trypsin (Promega) in an enzyme:protein ratio of 1:50. The protein aggregation was carried out in two steps of 1 min mixing at medium mixing speed, followed by a 10 min pause each. The sequential washes were performed in 2.5 min and slow speed, without releasing the beads from the magnet. The digestion was set to 4 h at 37 degrees with slow speed. The resulting peptides were analyzed by a nano-UHPLC-MS/MS system using an Ultimate 3000 RSLC coupled to an Orbitrap Q Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific Instrument). Elution was performed with an EASY spray column (75 μm × 50 cm, 2 μm particle size, Thermo Scientific) at a flow rate of 250 nL/min using a linear gradient of 2-45% solution B (80% acetonitrile –CAN-, 5% dimethylsulfoxide -DMSO-, 0.1% formic acid -FA- in H2O) in 50 min. Orbitrap detection was used for MS1 measurements at a resolving power of 70 K in a range between 375 and 1500 m/z with a 3∙106 automatic gain control (AGC) target and 50 ms maximum injection time (IT). Precursors were selected for data-independent fragmentation with an isolation window width of 34 m/z and 19 loop count. Higher collisional dissociation (HCD) energy was set to 27%, and MS2 scans were acquired at a resolution of 35 k, 3∙106 AGC target, and 50 ms maximum IT.

title: Propionic acid outperforms formic and acetic acid in MS sensitivity for high-flow reversed-phase LC-MS bottom-up proteomics (I)
projectDescription: The study aimed to assess the effect of substituting formic and acetic acids for propionic acid on electrospray ionization and chromatographic performance in reversed-phase LC-MS bottom-up proteomics. The deposit contains LC-MS data acquired at the Faculty of Pharmacy, Charles University, and Biomedical Research Centre, Hradec Králové, Czech Republic. To access the data from other facilities, please refer to the manuscript.
dataProcessingProtocol: The data from peptide mapping of bevacizumab were searched in Byonic v3.5 against the FASTA sequence downloaded from the Drug Bank and appended with common protein contaminants. The mass tolerance was 8 ppm for precursors and 18 ppm for fragments. A semitryptic cleavage with two missed cleavages was used. Oxidized Met, pyroGlu formation at N-terminal Glu and Gln, deamidated Asn, and dehydrated Asp were set as dynamic modifications. The search included a library of 132 human plasma N-glycans. Peptide-spectrum matches identified with a 2D FDR ≤ 1% were considered.  The data from DDA analyses of digested Jurkat and HeLa cell proteins were searched in Proteome Discoverer v2.3 using Byonic v3.5.0. The spectra were searched against the human protein database downloaded from UniProt (UP000005640). The mass tolerance was 7.5 ppm for precursors and 20 ppm for fragments. A semitryptic cleavage with one missed cleavage was used. Acetylated protein N-terminus, Oxidized Met, pyroGlu formation at N-terminal Glu and Gln, deamidated Asn, and dehydrated Asp were set as dynamic modifications. Carbamidomethylation of Cys was set as a fixed modification. Peptide-spectrum matches identified with a 2D FDR ≤ 1% were considered.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Bevacizumab was denatured in 5 M guanidinium chloride and reduced in 20 mM dithiothreitol for 30 min at room temperature. Thiols were not blocked. The mixture was diluted with the Low-Artifact Digestion Buffer (Merck/Sigma-Aldrich) containing dithiothreitol so that its concentration was 2 mM. The protein was digested by dimethylated SOLu-Trypsin added in a 1:20 enzyme-protein ratio at 37 °C for 2 hours. The digest was acidified with TFA, filtered, and desalted using the Pierce Peptide Desalting spin column (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The desalted peptides were vacuum-dried and reconstituted in 0.1% TFA and 0.001% PEG 20 000. The Jurkat cells (ATCC TIB-152) were cultured in 150 cm2 cultivation flasks (TPP) in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum. Cells were washed with phosphate-buffered saline and lysed on ice with 2.5% sodium deoxycholate containing 125 UI/mL benzonase. The protein concentration was determined using a bicinchoninic acid assay (Merck/Sigma Aldrich). One milligram of protein was buffered with 1 M Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, and reduced in 20 mM dithiothreitol for 30 min at room temperature. The free thiol groups were blocked using 50 mM chloroacetamide. The proteins were digested using dimethylated SOLu-trypsin in a 1:50 ratio at 37 °C overnight. The digest was acidified with TFA, and the precipitated deoxycholic acid was extracted using liquid-liquid extraction into ethyl acetate saturated with water. The supernatant was desalted using the Pierce Peptide Desalting spin columns. The desalted peptides were vacuum-dried and reconstituted in 0.1% TFA. Digests of HeLa cell line proteins were purchased from Thermo Fischer Scientific. LC-MS analyses were carried out using water/ACN mobile phases acidified with 0.1% FA, 0.5% AcA, or 0.5% PrA on nano- or analytical-flow LC-MS instruments.
